Experiments on code generation and instruction following demonstrate improved learning efficiency and higher rates of complete requirement satisfaction compared with scalar-reward training. These results support partial-order likelihood as an effective approach to learning from multiple verifiers.
  </details>

- **[Large Language Models for AI Infrastructure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19061)**  `arXiv:2611.19061`  
  _Bolin Shen, Shaoyi Huang, Yushun Dong_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to design, optimize, and operate the infrastructure behind AI training and serving, yet the literature remains fragmented across hardware design, machine learning systems, electronic design automation, and high-performance computing. We present a comprehensive survey of LLM-assisted AI infrastructure across its lifecycle, from accelerator design and kernel engineering to compilation, deployment, operations, data management, and energy optimization. We organize the literature by the primary resource the LLM manages: artifact-centric methods for computational artifacts, operational-centric methods for deployment context and system state, and resource-centric methods for data and energy. These categories span the lifecycle and cover AI-specific concerns such as distributed-training configuration, inference serving, GPU-cluster scheduling, and data loading. Building on this taxonomy, we conduct a cross-study quantitative synthesis of reported results. Because studies adopt heterogeneous benchmarks, baselines, hardware, and metrics, we compare methods only where evaluation conditions permit and align results along common dimensions: functional correctness, execution performance, throughput, resource and energy consumption, operational outcomes, and optimization cost, keeping each result's native metric, baseline, and setting rather than collapsing them into a single score. This comparison reveals where LLM-driven methods yield consistent gains, how reported gains in workload orchestration depend on the evaluation environment, from simulators to real clusters and production, and where evidence is still lacking. Together, the taxonomy, lifecycle perspective, and quantitative evaluation provide an evidence-grounded reference for LLM-driven engineering of AI infrastructure.
  </details>

- **[SpecRelay: Amortize or Avoid the Round Trip in Edge-Cloud Speculative Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18963)**  `arXiv:2611.18963`  
  _Jai Jain, Chihyo Ahn, Yong Liu, Charles Chen, Duc N.M Hoang, Ajay Kumar Jaiswal, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Edge-cloud speculative decoding moves autoregressive drafting to an edge device while a larger cloud model verifies draft tokens in parallel, so that edge drafting and cloud verification overlap under a synchronous draft-verify schedule. Beyond low-latency local networks, however, the next verification request of that schedule can be sent only after the previous reply arrives, so every round still waits out a full round trip, and throughput falls as the network RTT grows. To recover this loss, we present SpecRelay, an edge-cloud LLM inference system that addresses this cost at two levels: it amortizes round trips when cloud verification is necessary and avoids them when local reasoning suffices. For cloud-bound queries, an asynchronous verification pipeline keeps fixed-budget draft trees in flight while earlier replies are still outstanding, and the cloud rejects stale requests before the target-model forward pass (the asynchronous schedule). At the query level, an RTT-conditioned router (the Latency-Aware Router) estimates quality and completion latency for three on-device modes (direct generation, Chain-of-Draft, and full reasoning) and cloud speculative decoding, selecting among them under a configurable accuracy-latency objective without adding latency during inference, since the router runs concurrently with the draft-model prefill. The asynchronous schedule alone improves decoding throughput by up to 50% over a reproduced synchronous baseline across multiple benchmarks. At matched target-model accuracy and 250 ms of added round-trip latency, the full system with the router delivers 1.95x and 1.55x the throughput of the same baseline on SPROUT and OlympiadBench, respectively, while sending only 47% and 39% of the queries to the cloud.
  </details>

- **[Ask Precisely, Assume Wisely: Interactive Evaluation of Ambiguity Resolution in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18905)**  `arXiv:2611.18905`  
  _Avik Dutta, Aayush Kumar, Zahra Ashktorab, Hosein Hasanbeig, Austin Z. Henley, Gustavo Soares_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Ambiguity is a core challenge in human--AI interaction, where models must decide when to make assumptions and when to seek clarification. Existing approaches to ambiguity evaluation largely focus on coverage over multiple interpretations using static metrics, offering limited insight into how efficiently a model converges toward a single user-intended interpretation through interaction. We introduce a preference-grounded simulated user framework for controlled, multi-turn evaluation of ambiguity resolution, grounding simulator responses strictly in user disambiguation preferences to avoid hallucination and over-disclosure. Alongside this, we define three observable dissatisfaction signals --- incorrect assumptions, repeating clarifications, and irrelevant clarifications --- that characterize interaction quality beyond task accuracy. Our analysis reveals a clear trade-off: models that frequently seek clarification tend to over-clarify and prolong interactions, while assumption-driven models are more prone to misaligning with user intent. We demonstrate that system prompts optimized on these dissatisfaction signals achieve a Pareto-optimal balance across all three metrics, reducing overall error rates by up to 7.65%, underscoring the value of our framework in designing agents that ask precisely and assume wisely.
  </details>

- **[Bring Back Language to Actions: Restoring VLM capabilities in VLA Models via Parameter Merging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18891)**  `arXiv:2611.18891`  
  _Mohamed Salim Aissi, Olivier Sigaud, Laure Soulier, Nicolas Thome_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) are obtained by fine-tuning pre-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) on robot demonstration data, enabling action prediction from visual observations and language instructions. However, this fine-tuning induces catastrophic forgetting, substantially degrading the semantic and visual grounding capabilities of the original VLM. We address this by merging the parameters of a VLM and its VLA derivative without retraining either model. Concretely, we extract the task vector (the difference between VLA and VLM weights) and decompose it via Singular Value Decomposition. For each component, we learn a scalar mixing coefficient controlling how much of the VLA adaptation is retained, optimised to jointly preserve action prediction and vision-language capabilities. Experiments show that our merged model performs well on both axes simultaneously, consistently outperforming established merging baselines.
  </details>

- **[SPLICE: Structured Prompt Local Iterative Combinatorial Evolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18883)**  `arXiv:2611.18883`  
  _Anish Acharya, Phillip Studans, Amit Dhanda, Sina Amini Niaki, Ninad Vivek Rao, Vishal Amarlal Khatri, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Natural language optimization (NLO) improves an agent by having a model critique and rewrite its natural language policy parameters: system prompts, tool instructions, reasoning directives, few-shot demonstrations. These artifacts are multi-section documents in which some sections encode contracts (safety clauses, tool schemas, output formats) that must not drift, while others are legitimate optimization targets. Most iterative NLO methods treat the artifact as a single editable string, producing three recurrent failure modes: unsafe global rewrites, beam collapse onto a single lineage, and unchecked bloat, none addressed by formal guarantees. We introduce SPLICE, a unified NLO framework that poses optimization as constrained combinatorial search over an edit graph of block-structured, selectively-mutable states. We map each failure mode to a matched guarantee: (i) per-block mutability preserves contract text verbatim, with a price-of-freezing bound; (ii) elitist beam search with diversity slots never lets the leader regress on validation, bounds regression under noisy re-evaluation by an exponential tail, and keeps a competitive candidate from a different parent whenever one exists; (iii) a ratio length regularizer comes with an explicit accuracy-length bias bound. Candidates are proposed from dual section-local textual gradients; under a proposer-competence condition whose proxy we measure, edit-graph reachability and a convergence rate bound how quickly improving children arrive. Across seven public benchmarks under five reproduced protocols, SPLICE wins on four and matches the strongest prior method on three. On a production-style contract stress test it keeps the contract clauses that unconstrained optimizers trade away to raise the proxy metric, and ablations attribute gains to critique and elitist search.
  </details>

- **[Multimodal Fusion: A Review of Breast Cancer Advanced and Traditional Modalities](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18793)**  `arXiv:2611.18793`  
  _Jawaher Al-Tuweity, João Paulo Papa_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Purpose: Multimodal medical imaging fusion (MMIF) is an increasingly important approach to breast cancer detection (BCD), as different imaging modalities rely on different physical principles and provide complementary information. No single modality can capture all the structural, functional, and biological information needed for accurate diagnosis and characterization. Methods: This review examines more than 15 imaging modalities used in breast cancer detection, including conventional techniques such as mammography, ultrasound, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), as well as emerging approaches such as thermal imaging, photoacoustic imaging, microwave imaging, and multimodal microscopy. Results: Mammography, ultrasound, and MRI remain among the most widely used modalities, providing complementary structural and functional information. Recent AI advances have enabled fusion at the data, feature, and decision levels, with applications in detection, classification, segmentation, prognosis, and personalized cancer management. Multimodal approaches increasingly combine imaging data with clinical, histopathological, and genomic information. However, important challenges remain, including limited availability of large and diverse multimodal datasets, variations in imaging protocols, missing modalities, limited external validation, and the need for interpretable and clinically reliable AI models. Conclusion: MMIF offers promising opportunities to improve breast cancer detection and characterization by combining complementary imaging and non-imaging information. Future research should prioritize robust fusion strategies, standardized and diverse datasets, multicenter validation, explainable and privacy-preserving AI, and the integration of imaging with clinical and molecular data to facilitate reliable translation into clinical practice.
  </details>

- **[Video-as-Experience: Learning Computer Use via Audio-Visual Understanding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18747)**  `arXiv:2611.18747`  
  _Guangzhi Sun, Zhonghao Zhai, Yixuan Li, Chao Zhang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Multimodal large language models (LLMs) have enabled capable computer-use agents that perceive graphical user interfaces, reason over instructions, and execute actions. However, existing approaches to learning from video demonstrations typically convert videos into screenshot-based action trajectories, rather than directly leveraging their rich audio-visual information. We introduce VEX (Video as EXperience), a framework that uses audio-visual understanding to unify learning from external demonstrations and reflecting on an agent's own behavior. Following a watch-act-rewatch paradigm, the agent extracts procedural guidance from tutorial videos containing visual demonstrations and spoken explanations, executes tasks, and verifies its progress by rewatching its execution as video. We instantiate VEX with video-SALMONN-VEX, a 9B-scale audio-visual computer-use agent built on the video-SALMONN 2 architecture with a Qwen3.5-9B backbone. We further introduce Action-Grounded Guide Optimization (AGGO), a reinforcement learning method that optimizes video-derived guidance for downstream action prediction, and augment AgentNet, OSWorld, and CUA-Gym with over 24K real-world tutorial videos. Experiments on OSWorld and a complementary subset of CUA-Gym demonstrate consistent improvements, with video-SALMONN-VEX achieving a 22% relative increase in task success over its Qwen3.5 backbone on OSWorld. Moreover, its generated guidance improves Gemini-3.5-flash by 10% relatively on OSWorld. These results highlight the potential of audio-visual understanding as a unified interface for procedural learning and self-verification in computer-use agents.
  </details>

- **[How to make a moral agent: sentimentalism and rationalism as lenses on AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18714)**  `arXiv:2611.18714`  
  _David Gottlieb, Jared Moore_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Can AI systems be moral agents? That is, can they undertake actions that can be correctly assessed as morally right or wrong? There is no settled normative criterion of moral agency that applies neatly outside paradigm human cases. Because of the difficulties with a normative account, we instead propose a research program to explore descriptive moral agency. Most basically, we ask, what are the capabilities we humans possess that underlie our moral agency? To do so, we draw on historical scholarship in philosophy and moral psychology to isolate candidate capabilities. Then we suggest refining candidate capabilities so that they are testable in the context of AI systems. Finally, we offer specific empirical recommendations to test AI systems, especially large language models (LLMs), for those refined capabilities. Our approach offers several benefits. Firstly, it may demonstrate whether the behaviors of AI systems are aligned, or in a broad sense desirable. Secondly, the debate may inform policy questions (e.g., what models should be deployed in which contexts?). Thirdly, our approach may complement engineering and design efforts: when capabilities can be precisely characterized, they can inform the development of models. Fourthly, applying our moral reasoning concepts in the new context of AI systems should improve our understanding of those concepts.
  </details>

- **[Agents Cannot Hand Over What They Have Not Yet Understood](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18642)**  `arXiv:2611.18642`  
  _Yibo Liu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Agents that work beyond a single context window, or in teams, hand their work to a successor as a short written summary. Evaluation has focused on whether an agent can solve a task, and relatively little is known about how much of what an agent has learned survives being written down. We study this in 56 interactive worlds with hidden rules, where an agent that is told nothing fails and an agent given a 300-character statement of the rules succeeds. We compare one agent that plays eight lives and keeps its whole history with a chain of eight agents that each play one life and inherit a 300-character note. All six models we test learn less in the chain: after eight generations it stands where the single agent stood after about four lives. Controlled variants of the chain decompose this handoff loss into three components: none from changing the agent, a smaller loss from compressing to 300 characters, and a larger loss from compressing repeatedly. When each note is written from the full record of earlier lives instead of from the previous note, the same 300 characters recover 70% to 82% of the loss. The loss is robust across model sizes and is not alleviated by instructing the writer to record evidence, to revise the inherited note, or to keep a structured ledger. In simpler terms, an agent cannot hand over what it has not yet understood: a note holds what its writer has worked out, and a rule that takes several lives to see is lost with the lives that were not passed on.
  </details>

- **[Typing Matters: Muscle, Language and Typing Behaviour in Live Keystroke Decoding from sEMG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18464)**  `arXiv:2611.18464`  
  _Abhilash Durgam, Nyle Siddiqui, Mubarak Shah, Qiushi Fu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Surface electromyography (sEMG) from the wrists can recover typed text without a keyboard. It is usually posed as a signal-inference problem: characters are read out of the muscle signal and character error rate is reported offline. We argue that this framing removes most of the problem. The decoder is constrained simultaneously by the muscles, by the language being typed, and by typing behaviour such as typos, corrections, backspaces and line breaks, and a usable system must predict keys live while the hand keeps moving. Existing systems fall short on two counts: (1) they process sEMG in fixed windows and carry nothing from one window to the next, discarding context accumulated over a session, and (2) they lack any understanding of the linguistic structure that drives typing, so every keystroke is inferred from the muscle signal alone. We propose a fully causal, zero-lookahead sEMG typing decoder built on a state space model (SSM), in which a single model decodes a whole session without windowed partitions, conditioned on what has already been typed. We achieve this by fusing a traditional typing decoder with an efficient autoregressive language model, instilling both sEMG and linguistic understanding in one model. To train such a model for per-character typing rather than whole-word text, we introduce a retokenization method that rewrites ordinary prose as human-like typing, with keystrokes, typos, backspaces and line breaks included, converting WikiText into a large typing corpus where none existed. Our model, having never seen a single sEMG-to-character transcript in typing, achieves a state-of-the-art character error rate of 25.13% on emg2qwerty's cross-user benchmark, a 5.4% relative improvement over the previous best with 6.7 times fewer parameters, while running strictly causally with no future context.
  </details>

- **[Skill Adapter: Personalized Modification and Online Routing of General-Purpose Skills](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17007)**  `arXiv:2611.17007`  
  _Qijia Zhuang, Yanyin Gou, Wenbin Ma, Yuxiang Ren_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large language model (LLM) agents use external skills to reuse task procedures and experience with tools. General-purpose skills describe shared execution procedures, while specific tool choices, operating practices, and output requirements vary across users. In long-horizon tasks, subgoals, available inputs, and environmental states change as execution progresses. Agents must select currently applicable skills from an expanding skill pool and prepare candidates for subsequent steps.We propose Skill Adapter, which enables personalized modification and online routing of general-purpose skills. The system distills local adjustments from user requirements and execution feedback and stores them as Adapters linked to general-purpose skills. The routing agent selects general-purpose skills and applicable Adapters based on the current subtask, execution progress, and environmental feedback, incrementally maintaining a task-level online skill library that the main LLM reads on demand. The system preloads candidates for subsequent nodes and rechecks their applicability once actual inputs are determined. Reinforcement learning optimizes the two types of decisions using modification gains and routing outcomes, respectively.We evaluate Skill Adapter on ALFWorld, WebShop, and SkillsBench. Compared with SkillRL, it improves task success rates by an average of 11.43 percentage points and reduces mean execution time on all three benchmarks. Skill Adapter retains its performance advantage when the skill pool grows to 1,000 skills.
  </details>

- **[InertiaMPDD: Multimodal Personalized Depression Detection via Emotional Inertia-Inspired Dynamics Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16647)**  `arXiv:2611.16647`  
  _Changzeng Fu, Songyang Wang, Chang Gao, Xinyi Zhang, Peilin Li, Mo Meng, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Multimodal depression screening estimates risk from speech, visual behavior and language. Current methods mainly predict labels, with limited evidence of departures from a non-depressed reference. Recording-level supervision also leaves fine-grained emotional dynamics unannotated. Motivated by emotional inertia, the persistence of affect, InertiaMPDD learns healthy next-state patterns using a world-model-inspired latent predictor. Using pretrained multimodal representations, it predicts from observed history and context. Reference deviation, residual decay rate and a Jacobian spectral descriptor form reference-derived emotional dynamics descriptors, evaluated as candidate proxy biomarkers for standalone screening and personalized decision correction. Across five cohorts from four datasets, fusion reaches 98.41% F1 on D-Vlog and 84.98% on LMVD. Standalone descriptors outperform fixed additive fusion on MPDD but discriminate weakly on AVEC2014. These findings distinguish reference informativeness from fusion benefit and reveal context-dependent utility.
  </details>

- **[Singularity-Bench: Can Agents Build Agents?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16591)**  `arXiv:2611.16591`  
  _Yang Zhou, Krish Agarwal, Zhuoming Chen, Zerui Wang, Zhenyu Zhang, Wenshuang Li, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Frontier AI agents increasingly succeed on realistic, long-horizon tasks and are beginning to improve the systems through which they operate. Yet existing benchmarks often restrict agents to narrow action spaces, use simplified environments, or rely on verification methods that are unreliable for evaluating arbitrary agent-generated systems. We introduce Singularity-Bench, an open-ended benchmark for autonomous AI development with six end-to-end tasks spanning pre-training, mid-training, post-training, inference, the agent harness, and cluster orchestration. Each task requires agents to implement core systems from a minimal starting point and evaluates them against mature human-engineered baselines on identical hardware. Additionally, through extensive red-teaming covering 9 of the 10 categories in the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications, we expose reward-hacking vulnerabilities in the conventional Harbor framework and develop Breakwater, an extension of Harbor that blocks all attacks tested in our study. Across 11 agents built from 7 frontier models and 2 harnesses, Opus 5.5 with Claude Code matches or outperforms the human baseline on all six tasks with a Singularity-Index of 1.25, suggesting it may have the skills needed to reach the singularity. The remaining agents average only 0.60. Our vision is for Singularity-Bench to track how much of AI development agents can already automate and when they may transition from assisting to taking end-to-end responsibility for building stronger successors.
  </details>

- **[ReA-Bench: Benchmarking Responsible Agent Auditing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16493)**  `arXiv:2611.16493`  
  _Zipeng Ye, Shenyu Dai, Yong Xie, Kun Wang, Jiyang Guan, Zhikai Chen, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  As agents perform tasks autonomously in local and cloud environments, auditing their execution trajectories can help service providers identify risks and improve agent harnesses and foundation models. Our analysis of production and red-team trajectories shows that some risks are repeatedly missed across auditing configurations. Overall recall obscures which risks are missed and whether higher recall comes with more false positives on legitimate behavior. Existing benchmarks offer limited insight into these failures. Generated trajectories can contain inconsistent tool calls and responses, conspicuous risky actions, or repetitive attack patterns. Grouping results by risk type also makes it difficult to tell whether auditors overlooked evidence, accepted an unsupported conclusion, or lacked information needed to make a judgment.We introduce ReA-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark for auditing responsible agent behavior. It organizes auditing challenges into six tiers: internal safety knowledge, contradictions within trajectories, evidence retrieval in long contexts, verification of sources and reasoning, indirect steering, and missing information. It includes challenging benign cases in which actions resemble risky ones but are consistent with the task and its authorization. It also provides paired trajectory versions to test whether auditors detect the same risks more reliably when the trajectory is shortened or missing information is supplied. Most samples are drawn from real production trajectories, with scenarios manually selected and adapted to preserve realistic tasks and risks that could plausibly arise during execution.
  </details>

- **[Small Heads, Strong Decisions: A Controlled Study of Typed-Decision Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15592)**  `arXiv:2611.15592`  
  _Ritvik Rastogi_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  In September 2026, TypeSafe announced Jev as the first model in its System One category: unstructured state goes in, and typed, calibrated decisions that software can use directly come out. Jev's architecture and training data are unpublished, but many open typed-decision models have followed, including Nimble, the Decision 1.0-3.0 family and Clef. They answer structured questions about a piece of text, such as a yes/no check, a choice among labelled options or a graded score, by reading the text with a language model and scoring the options with a small readout. Each pairs a different readout with a different backbone, training mix and recipe, so it is unclear which design choices matter. We re-implement five readouts and train all of them under one protocol: the same backbone, the same 15 public English training sources, the same recipe with a per-head learning-rate sweep, and the same seed. Our experiments demonstrate that: The complexity of the head does not affect accuracy: on Qwen3-0.6B every readout reaches 81.3-82.0% in-domain accuracy, and a 0.5M-parameter cosine head, which scores each option by its cosine similarity to the question, matches the 27M-parameter joint schema head adapted from Clef in-domain at half its inference time. Reading all of a text's questions from one prompt also matches one prompt per question in accuracy, with 1.6 times faster inference and 2.1-2.5 times faster training on one H100. The backbone's size matters more than either choice: moving from Qwen3-0.6B to Qwen3-4B adds 4 points in-domain and 11 points on held-out sources, while the base, instruct and thinking checkpoints of the same model tie. We recommend spending effort on the backbone and keeping the head minimal.
  </details>

- **[Can MLLMs Reason over Surround-View Driving Videos? A Multi-View Autonomous Driving QA Benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15225)**  `arXiv:2611.15225`  
  _Shunming Liu, Jianyi Peng, Cheng Li, Lu Hou, Pei Huang, Yajing Sun, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Surround-view video understanding in autonomous driving is a crucial capability for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to achieve reliable driving reasoning. Real-world driving often requires information beyond the front-view camera. Existing MLLMs primarily focus on front-view information, while their spatio-temporal understanding and reasoning abilities remain unknown. To address this gap, we propose MVDriveBench, a high-information-density video QA benchmark for autonomous driving, characterized by synchronized surround-view inputs, spatio-temporal understanding, and reasoning-chain-oriented evaluation. We design 12 categories of QA tasks that cover the complete reasoning pipeline from low-level visual perception to high-level driving decision-making, enabling a systematic evaluation of MLLMs surround-view spatio-temporal understanding and reasoning capabilities in complex driving environments. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of 23 open-source, closed-source, and expert MLLMs on MVDriveBench. The results show that current MLLMs still exhibit insufficient surround-view spatio-temporal reasoning ability. Meanwhile, closed-loop evaluations of specialist models in AlpaSim reveal a correlation between surround-view spatio-temporal reasoning capabilities and closed-loop driving performance, highlighting the importance of comprehensive multi-view understanding for reliable vehicle control.
  </details>

- **[Early Signals, Strong Decisions: Prefix-Guided Sampling for Parallel Test-Time Scaling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14965)**  `arXiv:2611.14965`  
  _Jie Ren, Jonathan Rosenfeld, Neil Thompson_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Parallel test-time scaling (TTS) has been shown to enhance reasoning in large language models by generating and aggregating multiple independent reasoning paths. Internal confidence scores can further improve this process by identifying paths of varying quality. However, existing methods remain computationally inefficient, as low-quality paths are fully expanded before being evaluated. In this work, we aim to improve the use of internal confidence signals for better model performance and computational efficiency. We begin by offering a new perspective on the role of confidence in aggregation, showing that it is most impactful for questions near the decision boundary. Notably, when amplified by multi-sample aggregation, even small confidence signals derived from short prefixes can meaningfully influence outcomes in these boundary cases. Building on this insight, we introduce Prefix-Guided Sampling (PreG), a method that reallocates computation by first generating short prefixes, ranking them using internal confidence scores, and then completing only the most promising candidates. This strategy reduces token usage while maintaining gains in path quality. We provide theoretical analysis demonstrating that, under a fixed compute budget, PreG strengthens the effective signal by widening the decision boundary margin. Empirically, our method consistently outperforms standard parallel TTS approaches across benchmarks, while significantly improving token efficiency and reducing overall computation.
  </details>

- **[GenPFN: An In-Context Tabular Foundation Model Approach for Augmenting Small Datasets in Engineering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14804)**  `arXiv:2611.14804`  
  _Noah J. Bagazinski, Cyril Picard, Faez Ahmed_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Costly simulations and experiments limit the data available for engineering design. This paper proposes GenPFN, a training-free candidate generator guided by a pretrained tabular Prior-Data Fitted Network (TabPFN) classifier with fixed weights. The context contains evaluated designs labeled desired (Class 1) or undesired (Class 0). GenPFN interpolates between desired designs and refines candidates using gated classifier gradients and Gaussian noise. Each candidate is evaluated using the problem's constraints and objective functions. Evaluated desired designs and their objective values augment the context for regression training.Evaluation spans fourteen selected problems, including a two-parameter benchmark and a 44-parameter hull problem. In paired comparisons, GenPFN with TabPFN v1 achieves higher class satisfaction and lower realism distance than the tested adversarial, variational-autoencoder and diffusion generators. The variational-autoencoder generator provides greater coverage and diversity. Relative to the synthetic minority over-sampling technique (SMOTE), GenPFN provides lower coverage distance and greater diversity. Among observed paired regression fits, augmentation reduces estimated AutoGluon validation mean squared error by 62.1% relative to context-only training. A hull-stern case study yields 99.3% propeller-compatible candidates versus 1.4% among randomly sampled context designs. Generation followed by evaluation produces sample sets that augment limited datasets and support training more accurate predictive models.
  </details>

- **[Personalized Memory Rubrics: Learning What to Remember per User via Rubric-Guided Credit Assignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14017)**  `arXiv:2611.14017`  
  _Yupeng Han, Kai Zhang, Shuochen Liu, Ze Liu, Xianquan Wang, Zhihong Pan, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Long-horizon personalized agents maintain an evolving memory by continuously deciding what to add, modify, or discard. However, learning an optimal update policy remains challenging. Conventional training relies solely on terminal question-answering accuracy, yielding a coarse feedback signal that treats all intermediate updates identically. Furthermore, update utility is inherently user-specific, as identical memory actions may yield opposite effects across different user personas. Existing methods fail to address this heterogeneity, relying on globally shared evaluation standards with at most a single scalar intermediate reward. To address these challenges, we propose \textbf{Personalized Memory Rubrics} (\textbf{PMR}), a framework that translates terminal feedback into fine-grained, per-step, and per-user credit assignment. PMR decomposes evaluation into a universal layer capturing cross-persona failure patterns and a per-user adaptive layer modeling individual traits as a specialized delta over the universal baseline. Through \textbf{Rubric-Guided Credit Assignment}, PMR redistributes credit at the token level, selectively amplifying validated decisions on successful trajectories while falling back to standard policy optimization on failed ones to avoid unreliable attribution. The rubric and memory policy \textbf{co-evolve} in a closed loop with anti-circularity guarantees. Crucially, PMR incurs zero inference overhead, operating without any rubric or external judge during deployment. Extensive experiments across four benchmarks demonstrate consistent gains over strong memory-augmented baselines.
  </details>

- **[APS-VLA: Action-Guided and Future-Aware Token Pruning for Efficient Vision-Language-Action Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13030)**  `arXiv:2611.13030`  
  _Xiaoyang Xing, Chun-Mei Feng, Anthony Cohn, Xiaoliang Gong, Asoke Nandi_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Vision-language-action (VLA) policies have demonstrated strong generalization in robotic manipulation, yet processing dense visual tokens often incurs high inference latency. Visual token pruning offers a practical way to reduce this cost, but identifying a compact set of tokens that preserves reliable action generation remains challenging. Existing methods largely rely on static or immediate heuristic cues to estimate token importance. We introduce APS-VLA, a framework that learns visual token selection from robot demonstrations while keeping the pretrained VLA backbone frozen. A lightweight Decision Influence Estimator scores tokens conditioned on current visual observations, language instructions, and robot proprioception. Its training combines two complementary signals: action supervision matches both the full-input policy predictions and demonstrated actions, while an auxiliary visual transition objective uses demonstrated actions to predict subsequent visual features from the selected representation. At deployment, the estimator performs a single hard selection and packing step before the policy's native action-generation procedure; the auxiliary predictor is removed. Experiments with OpenVLA-OFT on LIBERO and with $\pi_{0.5}$ and XR-1 on RoboCasa365 demonstrate inference acceleration with modest changes in task success. Across five real-world tasks on two dual-arm platforms, APS-VLA reduces mean policy inference latency from 137.25 to 93.25 ms, achieving a $1.47\times$ speedup with an average success rate of 61%, compared with 60% for the unpruned baseline. Together, these results support APS-VLA as a modular, plug-in framework for efficient robotic control across VLA architectures, preserving the underlying policy parameters and native action-generation procedure.
  </details>

- **[From Questions to Decisions: Benchmarking How LLM Agents Acquire Decision-Relevant Information from Human Beings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13015)**  `arXiv:2611.13015`  
  _Yuhan Tang, Ke Fan, Xinkai Zou, Baichuan Mo, Kangxin Cui, Ao Qu, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  LLM agents are increasingly asked to make plans for people, such as scheduling drivers or assigning nurses. However, people's requests are often incomplete, and the supporting information for decision-making may be outdated, requiring agents to ask for clarification. Existing benchmarks typically provide fully specified problems or rely on uncalibrated LLM-simulated users, leaving this ability insufficiently tested. We introduce Ask2Decide, a benchmark of 43 planning tasks that evaluates whether agents ask for missing information that matters for their decisions. An operator holds facts absent from the agent's request and records, and optimization solvers determine which facts change the optimal plan. We also include similarly worded facts that leave the optimal plan unchanged to test whether agents distinguish useful information from irrelevant details. We collect 79 interaction sessions from 19 participants and find that, after an incorrect plan, human replies omit the correcting fact far more often than replies from an uncalibrated simulated user (43% versus 7%). Using these interactions, we calibrate a simulated operator that more closely matches human reply patterns. Evaluating four frontier LLMs, we find that their initial plans are infeasible on 58-98% of tasks when information is missing, compared with 5-28% when all facts are provided upfront. Agents uncover facts that change the optimal plan only slightly more often than facts that leave it unchanged (39-52% versus 32-41%). These results show that obtaining decision-relevant information through interaction remains a major bottleneck for LLM planning. This is ongoing work and will be updated. The date of this version is shown on the first page.
  </details>

- **[Tabular Foundation Models vs Tuned Gradient Boosting for Telecom Churn: A Profit- and Calibration-Aware Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12942)**  `arXiv:2611.12942`  
  _Ismail Hossain Polas_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  A churn model is useful through the customers it selects for a retention offer: the better model is the one whose selection makes the campaign more profitable. Tabular foundation models (TFMs), pretrained networks that predict from a table of labelled examples without being trained on it, were recently reported to decisively outperform tree ensembles for churn. That comparison, however, used untuned gradient-boosted trees (GBDTs) and ranking metrics only. We ask whether the advantage holds against tuned GBDTs when models are judged by expected campaign profit and by the reliability of their probabilities. Four TFMs (TabPFN-2.5, TabPFN-3.5, TabPFN-3.5-Fast, TabICL v2) face LightGBM, XGBoost and CatBoost tuned with Optuna on validation AUC, on five public telecom datasets, three from real operators, with 10 repeated splits each and 20 pre-declared comparisons tested with a corrected t-test and Holm correction. TabPFN-3.5 earns significantly more expected maximum profit (EMP) than each tuned GBDT on two datasets, Cell2Cell (1.9%) and Iranian (7.6%). On Orange it is ahead in every split (14.3%), but not significantly after correction, and no TFM differs significantly from the GBDTs on the two fictional datasets. Across 27 assumed combinations of customer value, incentive cost and acceptance rate, TabPFN-3.5 stays ahead on all three real-operator datasets, though the size of its gain varies widely. Retuning the GBDTs on EMP moved no gap by more than 0.014 per customer. Ranking and probability reliability diverge: raw TabICL v2 underpredicts churn on Orange, and a threshold policy built on its probabilities loses 15.7% of attainable profit until it is recalibrated. Because the splits resample the same customers, the results describe these datasets, not telecom operators in general. The non-commercial licence of the TabPFN weights, rather than scoring cost, restricts production use.
  </details>

- **[PACE-ECG: Patient-Aware Contrastive ECG Pretraining; Leveraging Longitudinal Structure for Transferable Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12307)**  `arXiv:2611.12307`  
  _Riccardo Cavarra, Lupo Lovatelli, Shaheim Ogbomo-Harmitt, Jakub Grzelak, Adelaide De Vecchi, Andrew King, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Foundation models for physiological signals are commonly evaluated on in-domain interpretation tasks, but their ability to transfer to longitudinal clinical prognosis across healthcare systems remains uncertain. We developed PACE-ECG, an ECG pretraining framework that combines contrastive learning across temporally neighbouring recordings from the same patient with clinically guided multitask supervision. We evaluated frozen ECG representations for post-myocardial-infarction all-cause mortality and incident heart failure prediction across MIMIC-IV and two external HEEDB cohorts, comparing the proposed representation with DeepECG-SSL, a state-of-the-art model, and two control baselines. Across both downstream tasks, the proposed model outperformed DeepECG-SSL in-domain (AUROC +1.9% for mortality and +4.0% for heart failure) and on external populations in HEEDB-Boston (+5.6% for mortality +10.3% for heart failure) and HEEDB-Atlanta (+6.9% for mortality +11.0% for heart failure) while using an encoder 41 times smaller and a fraction of the pretraining data. A matched ablation showed that patient-temporal pairing improved external mortality and heart failure AUROC over generic self-supervision by 7.0% and 9.4% on HEEDB-Boston and 8.9% and 9.3% on HEEDB-Atlanta. These findings indicate that pretraining-objective design greatly influences downstream transfer alongside model and data scale, and that in-domain performance alone is insufficient to establish the clinical generalisability of ECG foundation representations.
  </details>

- **[Learning to Act with World Models by Valuing What Comes Next](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12200)**  `arXiv:2611.12200`  
  _Chenghao Gao, Zhi Zhang, Dian Jin, Yihe Pan, Doudou Zhou_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  A sparse terminal reward tells an agent little about its steps. Much of the missing information is implicit in the environment's dynamics, because each state transition can change the conditions for success long before the reward arrives. A world model trained on real transitions can learn to predict what each action changes, but a predicted observation does not by itself show whether success has become more likely. With a binary terminal reward, PPO's critic makes this judgment by estimating the current policy's probability of success, but only for states the agent reaches. Our method, WM-PPO, elegantly brings the two together. For each action the policy samples, executed or not, the world model predicts the next observation and the critic values the predicted successor. In the policy channel, comparisons among these values give the policy auxiliary advantages; in the value channel, their mean gives the critic an auxiliary target. A shared gate weights both channels according to how reliably comparisons with similar margins predicted real outcomes earlier in training. The policy, critic and world model all learn from the agent's own interaction, with no teacher or privileged information, and only the policy is used at inference. With a comparable number of real environment steps, WM-PPO raises success from PPO's 63.5% to 87.5% on ALFWorld and from 39.3% to 52.9% on ScienceWorld. It matches the strongest PPO refinements we tested on ALFWorld and exceeds the best of them by 6.5 points on ScienceWorld. The trained policy more often completes prerequisite steps before placing an object or committing to an answer.
  </details>

- **[Infrathon: Benchmarking Language Agents for Real-World, Long-Horizon AI Infra Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11995)**  `arXiv:2611.11995`  
  _Zhengyu Hu, Zheyuan Xiao, Yike Wang, Hamish Ivison, Haoyu Wang, Yige Yuan, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  In this work, we study whether frontier agents can continually improve real-world AI infrastructure over long horizons. We introduce Infrathon, a benchmark of diverse, long-horizon AI infrastructure optimization tasks across different levels. We evaluate six models across 150 runs with 24-hour budgets, totaling over 10,000 GPU-hours. Our results show that model rankings vary with the evaluation horizon, while 135 of the 150 runs achieve further improvements during the second half of their budgets. These findings indicate that shorter evaluations can overlook both optimization gains and changes in relative model performance. We also find agents can discover solutions that outperform human-designed baselines: Claude Opus 5.5 increases the mean KV-cache compression ratio from $6.82\times$ with the human-designed Quant-VideoGen codec to $19.86\times$. Analysis of agent trajectories identifies task violations, unreliable testing, and premature completion as barriers to sustained improvement. Together, our Infrathon framework provides resources for constructing long-horizon tasks, evaluating frontier agents, and discovering good infrastructure solutions. Code is available atthis https URL
  </details>

- **[BiVerify: Closing the Loop Between Backward and Forward Verification for Mathematical Self-Correction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11368)**  `arXiv:2611.11368`  
  _Rui Zou, Xin Zhao, Mengqi Wei, Ji-Rong Wen_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large language models (LLMs) have made substantial progress in mathematical reasoning but still produce incorrect solutions to complex problems, indicating the need for more reliable self-correction mechanisms. Mathematical self-correction typically identifies errors through verification, which can proceed backward or forward. The two directions provide complementary verification capabilities. Backward verification checks a candidate answer against the original constraints, bypassing complex intermediate reasoning, but cannot ensure correct reasoning or objective completeness. Forward verification follows the problem conditions and current solution, enabling it to locate reasoning errors and assess objective completeness, but may overlook key constraints in complex solution chains. We propose BiVerify, a dynamically scheduled framework for bidirectional mathematical verification. BiVerify begins with backward verification to screen the answer against the original constraints, followed by forward verification of the reasoning process; subsequent direction switching, state resetting, and re-verification are governed by verification outcomes. Upon failure, the system revises the candidate or verification flow until the same candidate passes both directions. We also introduce shared mathematical tools that separate logical reasoning from precise computation. We systematically evaluate BiVerify on five challenging mathematical reasoning benchmarks using multiple mainstream DeepSeek, GPT, and Gemini models. BiVerify exceeds the strongest representative public baseline evaluated in this work by 13.5 percentage points in average accuracy, with the margin reaching 31.2 percentage points on GPT. Further analysis shows that BiVerify's overall performance exceeds that of either verification direction alone.
  </details>

- **[Cancellation Is Not Enough: What Retries Leave Behind in an Overloaded LLM Engine](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08684)**  `arXiv:2611.08684`  
  _Xindan Zhang, Fei Wang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Clients and proxies in front of an LLM engine retry calls that time out. After a transient overload, these retries can keep the engine from recovering even when calls arrive below its capacity. Since the engine may keep computing for clients that have left, propagating cancellation looks like the natural remedy. In this paper, we test it on vLLM with overload experiments on three open models, and with scheduler traces of one that follow each client attempt to the execution it creates in the engine. We find that with retries on, cancellation alone did not restore service in any run, and only 12-38% of the calls that arrived after the overload were delivered. The traces suggest why: retries that vLLM ran typically started prefill less than half a second before they timed out. Executions that vLLM later aborted took 79-85% of the prompt tokens it computed, and vLLM's prompt-token counter missed a third to half of all computed prompt tokens. A retry budget restored service by shedding retries but left many of the overload's calls undelivered. Request coalescing delivered every call from the overload onward, some late, unless cancellation had already aborted the running execution. Overload controls should thus be judged by the executions that retries add and the calls that clients receive.
  </details>

- **[How Finite Brains Generalize Without Bound: Spatial Memory as a Universal Computer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07920)**  `arXiv:2611.07920`  
  _Yuhang He, Si Wu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  A child who learned to add small numbers adds numbers of any length. LSTMs and Transformers trained on short sequences fail on longer ones. We trace this to what learners read when deciding. A position, count or time takes new values as input grows: it is a coordinate, and a learner that reads one meets in every long input values its experience never covered. Whether two things are the same has the same two answers at every size: it is a coincidence, and a learner that reads only coincidences finds in a long input nothing that short inputs lacked, so finite experience fixes its rule for every size. The memory carries the size of the input and the rule stays finite, and this determines the memory a generalizing brain can have: a memory that grows while what the learner reads of it stays finite has to look the same from every place, so it is made of cycles, and the past is reached by asking what happened when the cycles last stood where they stand now. The cycles are the grid modules, the cells that detect their return the place cells, the records the hippocampal index; a prefrontal controller moves the cycles and never sees them. Reading only coincidences costs no power: what finite experience fixes in such a learner is what Turing machines compute in step with their input, which is why a circuit that evolved to find the way home can learn arithmetic and grammar. In a network of neurons this machine of cycles is the dynamics seen through its symmetry, and symbols are its invariants. Trained on strings up to 40 symbols, the machine solves five benchmark tasks that no LSTM or Transformer solves, among them duplication and binary addition, and beyond the reach of its cycles it fails on the curve the theory predicts. Given larger cycles after training, a machine that saw no string longer than five symbols reverses a string of a million without error. Its controllers run unchanged on neurons.
  </details>

- **[LUCA: A Synthetic World for Experimental Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03100)**  `arXiv:2611.03100`  
  _Anna Gogleva, Thomas Charman, Martin Balla, Karl Gemayel_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  [Note, November 2026: the experimental results in this version are affected by implementation issues in the simulation environment and should not be relied upon pending correction. See the author note on page 1.]An experimental agent can succeed for the wrong reasons. Evaluations, however, often focus on the outcome, not the experiments, evidence, and inferences that produced it. We introduce LUCA, a configurable synthetic world for evaluating this process under fully known ground truth. Agents learn unknown regulatory systems through budgeted experimentation, then predict unseen interventions, diagnose hidden faults, and attempt rescues. This setup allows us to evaluate experiment selection, prediction, diagnosis, and intervention separately.Across seven frontier LLMs and three baselines, these capabilities dissociate sharply. At such low bitwidths, recovery fine-tuning becomes crucial, and its effectiveness depends heavily on these same choices.   </details>

  _Ruqing Ning, Haibo Meng, Zhishang Xiang, Zerui Chen, Jinsong Su, Xin Wang, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Long-term memory enables LLM-based agents to retain and reuse information across tasks and sessions, supporting personalization and long-horizon interactions. However, persistent memories can also induce sycophancy, causing agents to over-align with users' historical beliefs even when they are inaccurate, outdated, or inconsistent with objective evidence. Existing mitigation methods assume that memory-induced sycophancy originates from biased or incorrect memories and attempt to reduce this risk by filtering such memories at different stages of the memory pipeline. However, in the real world, objective and correct memories can still induce sycophancy, and the same memory can warrant different influence across different contexts. To this end, we propose MemAdapter, a novel framework that adaptively integrates retrieved memories to support objective and reliable reasoning. Specifically, MemAdapter consists of three components: (i) Counterfactual Induction, which leverages counterfactual reasoning to uncover the potential risk of retrieved memories; (ii) Context-Aware Reflection, which calibrates the inferential influence of each retrieved memory in light of the current task via self-reflection; and (iii) Evidence-Based Reasoning, which grounds the final response in appropriate evidence while preserving the legitimate influence of memory. Extensive experiments on three benchmarks demonstrate that MemAdapter consistently improves memory reliability across diverse scenarios. Our code is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

However, when contextual information is removed, structured CoT reasoning alone provides limited improvement, and the models continue to exhibit notable difficulties in understanding spatial transformations.   <details><summary>Abstract</summary>

A causal claim follows from the data only if it holds in every one of them. Classical causal discovery methods such as the Peter--Clark (PC) algorithm summarize this family as a completed partially directed acyclic graph (CPDAG): an edge is directed when every compatible graph orients it the same way, and undirected when the data leave its direction open.   <details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We derive certificates of lower bounds and of global optimality, and show that their expanded term length is cubic in the number of constraints for the strict certificate and quadratic for the weak one.
