  _Neha Kalibhat, Zi Wang, Prasoon Bajpai, Drew Proud, Wenjun Zeng, Been Kim, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We introduce a black-box interpretability framework that learns a verifiable constitution: a natural language summary of how changes to a prompt affect a model's specific behavior, such as its alignment, correctness, or adherence to constraints. Our method leverages atomic concept edits (ACEs), which are targeted operations that add, remove, or replace an interpretable concept in the input prompt. By systematically applying ACEs and observing the resulting effects on model behavior across various tasks, our framework learns a causal mapping from edits to predictable outcomes. This learned constitution provides deep, generalizable insights into the model. Empirically, we validate our approach across diverse tasks, including mathematical reasoning and text-to-image alignment, for controlling and understanding model behavior. We found that for text-to-image generation, GPT-Image tends to focus on grammatical adherence, while Imagen 4 prioritizes atmospheric coherence. Moreover, our results show that the learned constitutions are highly effective for controlling model behavior, achieving an average of 1.86 times boost in success rate over methods that do not use constitutions. Our open-sourced code can be found atthis https URL
  </details>

  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large language models (LLMs) increasingly solve difficult problems by producing reasoning traces before emitting a final response. Furthermore, cross-model probing shows that even stronger models frequently repeat the source model's errors when given its partial reasoning trace, while allowing further reasoning substantially improves recovery. Together, these results provide a reproducible, model-agnostic measurement of reasoning trace dynamics that generalizes across answer formats and can reveal model-specific failure modes invisible to aggregate accuracy.
  </details>

  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  While tabular foundation models have achieved remarkable success in classification and regression, adapting them to model time-to-event outcomes for survival analysis is non-trivial due to right-censoring, where data observations may end before the event of interest occurs. We evaluate existing classification formulations, including hazard modeling and multi-class classification approaches, and introduce a new formulation that directly models cumulative failure probabilities at discretized time points, treating censored observations as examples with missing labels at certain time points. Our comparison provides practical guidance on when to use these models and which survival formulation to choose.
  </details>

- **[Flow Perturbation++: Multi-Step Unbiased Jacobian Estimation for High-Dimensional Boltzmann Sampling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.21177)**  `arXiv:2601.21177`  
  _Xin Peng, Ang Gao_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  The scalability of continuous normalizing flows (CNFs) for unbiased Boltzmann sampling remains limited in high-dimensional systems due to the cost of Jacobian-determinant evaluation, which requires $D$ backpropagation passes through the flow layers. Existing stochastic Jacobian estimators such as the Hutchinson trace estimator reduce computation but introduce bias, while the recently proposed Flow Perturbation method is unbiased yet suffers from high variance. We present \textbf{Flow Perturbation++}, a variance-reduced extension of Flow Perturbation that discretizes the probability-flow ODE and performs unbiased stepwise Jacobian estimation at each integration step. This multi-step construction retains the unbiasedness of Flow Perturbation while achieves substantially lower estimator variance. Integrated into a Sequential Monte Carlo framework, Flow Perturbation++ achieves significantly improved equilibrium sampling on a 1000D Gaussian Mixture Model and the all-atom Chignolin protein compared with Hutchinson-based and single-step Flow Perturbation baselines.
  </details>

- **[What Does a Cosine of 0.8 Mean? Monotone Calibration of Embedding Similarity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.16907)**  `arXiv:2601.16907`  
  _Nicolas Tacheny_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Text embedding models turn sentences into vectors, and the cosine between two vectors is the usual measure of their similarity. Search, semantic caching and deduplication often accept a pair when this cosine reaches a fixed threshold. When people judge one pair of sentences more similar than another, the cosine usually agrees, but its value means different things for different models, because each model packs its scores into its own narrow range. The same threshold can therefore keep most pairs with one model and few with another.We propose to calibrate the score instead of changing the model. An increasing function fitted on sentence pairs rated by people translates the cosine of each model into the human rating scale and never reverses the order of two pairs.We fit three such functions for six models, ranging from a simple S-shaped curve to a free step function. On new pairs, calibrated scores agree with human ratings and the models agree with one another. One threshold selects pairs of similar quality whatever the model. The scale obtained belongs to the human ratings used to fit it, so its values shift on two datasets rated differently while the models stay comparable.
  </details>

- **[Micro-Macro Tensor Neural Surrogates for Uncertainty Quantification in Collisional Plasma](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24205)**  `arXiv:2512.24205`  
  _Wei Chen, Giacomo Dimarco, Lorenzo Pareschi_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Plasma kinetic equations exhibit pronounced sensitivity to microscopic perturbations in model parameters and data, making reliable and efficient uncertainty quantification (UQ) essential for predictive simulations. However, the cost of uncertainty sampling, the high-dimensional phase space, and multiscale stiffness pose severe challenges to both computational efficiency and error control in traditional numerical methods. These aspects are further emphasized in presence of collisions where the high-dimensional nonlocal collision integrations and conservation properties pose severe constraints. To overcome this, we present a variance-reduced Monte Carlo framework for UQ in the Vlasov--Poisson--Landau (VPL) system, in which neural network surrogates replace the multiple costly evaluations of the Landau collision term. The method couples a high-fidelity, asymptotic-preserving VPL solver with inexpensive, strongly correlated surrogates based on the Vlasov--Poisson--Fokker--Planck (VPFP) and Euler--Poisson (EP) equations. For the surrogate models, we introduce a generalization of the separable physics-informed neural network (SPINN), developing a class of tensor neural networks based on an anisotropic micro-macro decomposition, to reduce velocity-moment costs, model complexity, and the curse of dimensionality. To further increase correlation with VPL, we calibrate the VPFP model and design an asymptotic-preserving SPINN whose small- and large-Knudsen limits recover the EP and VP systems, respectively. Numerical experiments show substantial variance reduction over standard Monte Carlo, accurate statistics with far fewer high-fidelity samples, and lower wall-clock time, while maintaining robustness to stochastic dimension.
  </details>

- **[CLARiTy: A Vision Transformer for Multi-Label Classification and Weakly-Supervised Localization of Chest X-ray Pathologies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.16700)**  `arXiv:2512.16700`  
  _John M. Statheros, Hairong Wang, Richard Klein_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Chest X-ray interpretation requires multi-label classification and spatial localization, yet region-level annotations are scarce, so weakly supervised localization involves training on image-level labels to produce class heatmaps. The step that converts heatmaps into boxes is rarely calibrated, that is, fitted on validation images, and localization results seldom leave the training dataset. We present CLARiTy (Class Localizing and Attention Refining Image Transformer), a vision transformer whose class tokens yield class-specific attention maps without gradient class activation mapping. A SegmentCAM head trained on anatomical region masks, not pathology masks, suppresses background. OneBox then converts the heatmaps into boxes, with parameters fitted per finding and resolution. On the official NIH split, CLARiTy outperforms the compared methods at matched resolution in localization and remains competitive in classification. Against published ThoraX-PriorNet values at matched 224 px resolution, the relative gain in macro intersection-over-union (IoU) accuracy at IoU 0.5 is 50.7%. The largest relative gain is on nodules: at that threshold the 224-pixel model reaches 0.154, where no compared method exceeds 0.013. Without training any weights on RSNA Pneumonia or VinDr-CXR, we refit only the OneBox parameters on target validation images, leaving the model and heatmaps unchanged. Localization is competitive with RAD-DINO and ahead of TorchXRayVision DenseNet121-NIH at every threshold. Fitting the box extractor on validation images, freezing it before testing and reporting localization across thresholds gives a protocol that carries to new corpora without retraining the model. Code is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Adaptive Layer-Wise Transformations for Post-Training Quantization of Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.17809)**  `arXiv:2511.17809`  
  _Cuong Pham, Hoang Anh Dung, Cuong C. Nguyen, Trung Le, Gustavo Carneiro, Jianfei Cai, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large language models require significant computational resources for deployment, making quantization essential for practical applications. However, the main obstacle to effective quantization lies in systematic outliers in activations and weights, which cause substantial LLM performance degradation, especially at low-bit settings. While existing transformation-based methods like affine and rotation transformations successfully mitigate outliers, they apply the homogeneous transformation setting, i.e., using the same transformation types across all layers, ignoring the heterogeneous distribution characteristics within LLMs. In this paper, we propose an adaptive transformation selection framework that systematically determines optimal transformations on a per-layer basis. To this end, we first formulate transformation selection as a differentiable optimization problem to achieve the accurate transformation type for each layer. However, searching for optimal layer-wise transformations for every model is computationally expensive. To this end, we establish the connection between weight distribution kurtosis and accurate transformation type. Specifically, we propose an outlier-guided layer selection method using robust $z$-score normalization that achieves comparable performance to differentiable search with significantly reduced overhead. Comprehensive experiments on LLaMA family models demonstrate that our adaptive approach consistently outperforms the widely-used fixed transformation settings. For example, our method achieves an improvement of up to 4.58 perplexity points and a 2.11% gain in average six-task zero-shot accuracy under aggressive W3A3KV2 quantization settings for the LLaMA-3-8B model compared to the current best existing method, FlatQuant, demonstrating the necessity of heterogeneous transformation selection for optimal LLM quantization.
  </details>

- **[A Systematic Analysis of Out-of-Distribution Detection Under Representation and Training Paradigm Shifts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.11934)**  `arXiv:2511.11934`  
  _Claudio César Claros Olivares, Austin J. Brockmeier_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We present a systematic benchmark of out-of-distribution (OOD) detection confidence scoring functions (CSFs) through a representation-centric lens. Our study spans CNN and ViT backbones, multiple training paradigms, four image-classification source datasets (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SuperCIFAR-100, and TinyImageNet), and OOD datasets grouped into near, mid, and far regimes based on CLIP-derived semantic distances. To compare CSFs across these settings, we employ a rank-based pipeline of Friedman and Conover tests that identifies top cliques of statistically indistinguishable winners under threshold-free ranking metrics (AURC and AUGRC). The main empirical finding is that the family of CSFs that are competitive detectors correlates with characteristics of the learned representation. For both CNNs and ViTs, simple probabilistic scores dominate misclassification detection. On CNNs, margin-based scores are strongest in near-OOD regimes, while geometry-aware scores such as NNGuide, fDBD, and CTM become more competitive as shift severity increases. On fine-tuned ViTs, the top cliques are led mainly by reconstruction- and residual-based scores. To interpret these ranking shifts, we analyze the last-layer representation using Neural Collapse (NC) metrics. The resulting picture is consistent across architectures: prototype- and boundary-aware scores become stronger when the representation is more collapsed and better aligned with classifier weights, whereas weaker-collapse regimes favor gradient- and manifold-based scores. Building on these insights, we propose two contributions: a simple PCA-based projection-filtering procedure that improves detector performance, and an approach that uses only the NC measurements of a trained classifier to predict its competitive out-of-distribution detector shortlist, without OOD data for that classifier and without knowledge of the shift.
  </details>

- **[Chance-constrained Flow Matching for High-Fidelity Constraint-aware Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.25157)**  `arXiv:2509.25157`  
  _Jinhao Liang, Yixuan Sun, Anirban Samaddar, Sandeep Madireddy, Ferdinando Fioretto_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Generative models excel at synthesizing high-fidelity samples from complex data distributions, but they often violate hard constraints arising from physical laws or task specifications. A common remedy is to project intermediate samples onto the feasible set at each sampling step. However, repeated projection can disrupt the learned sampling dynamics because this feasible set is defined for clean samples rather than noisy intermediate states. Thus, recent studies first estimate clean samples and then project them to the feasible set, but this increases algorithmic complexity and accumulates errors across steps. To address these issues, this paper proposes Chance-constrained Flow Matching (CCFM), a training-free method that formulates constraint enforcement during sampling as stochastic optimization while retaining the hard-constraint feasibility guarantee of projection-based methods. By avoiding direct projection of noisy intermediate states onto the clean-sample feasible set, CCFM mitigates the distributional distortion. Unlike approaches that first estimate and project clean samples, CCFM avoids complex multi-stage procedures. Experiments show that CCFM outperforms current state-of-the-art constrained generative models in modeling complex physical systems governed by partial differential equations, molecular docking problems, and physics-informed motion generation, delivering superior feasibility and fidelity.
  </details>

- **[Space Group Conditional Flow Matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.23822)**  `arXiv:2509.23822`  
  _Omri Puny, Yaron Lipman, Benjamin Kurt Miller_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Inorganic crystals are periodic, highly-symmetric arrangements of atoms in three-dimensional space. Their structures are constrained by the symmetry operations of a crystallographic \emph{space group} and restricted to lie in specific affine subspaces known as \emph{Wyckoff positions}. The frequency an atom appears in the crystal and its rough positioning are determined by its Wyckoff position. Most generative models that predict atomic coordinates overlook these symmetry constraints, leading to unrealistically high populations of proposed crystals exhibiting limited symmetry. We introduce Space Group Conditional Flow Matching, a novel generative framework that samples significantly closer to the target population of highly-symmetric, stable crystals. We achieve this by conditioning the entire generation process on a given space group and set of Wyckoff positions; specifically, we define a conditionally symmetric noise base distribution and a group-conditioned, equivariant, parametric vector field that restricts the motion of atoms to their initial Wyckoff position. Our form of group-conditioned equivariance is achieved using an efficient reformulation of \emph{group averaging} tailored for symmetric crystals. Importantly, it reduces the computational overhead of symmetrization to a negligible level. We achieve state of the art results on crystal structure prediction and de novo generation benchmarks. We also perform relevant ablations.
  </details>

- **[Autonomous Learning From Success and Failure: Goal-Conditioned Supervised Learning with Negative Feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.03206)**  `arXiv:2509.03206`  
  _Zeqiang Zhang, Fabian Wurzberger, Gerrit Schmid, Sebastian Gottwald, Daniel A. Braun_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Learning from reward functions and imitation learning of demonstrations are the two principal approaches for training autonomous systems that interact with an environment through action and observation. Both, however, require human specification for each behaviour to be acquired, a problem for long-lived self-adaptive systems whose goals and operating conditions cannot be fully anticipated at design time. Recently, Goal-Conditioned Supervised Learning (GCSL) through self-imitation has been proposed as a self-supervised alternative: by strategically relabelling goals, agents can derive policy insights from their own experiences. Despite its successes, this framework presents two notable limitations: (1) learning exclusively from self-generated experiences can exacerbate the agents' inherent biases; (2) the relabelling strategy allows agents to focus solely on successful outcomes, precluding them from learning from their mistakes. To address these issues, we propose GCSL with Negative Feedback (GCSL-NF), which evaluates each trajectory twice: positively with respect to relabelled goals, and correctively with respect to the goal originally intended. The corrective target comes from a similarity function learned contrastively from trajectory-induced neighbourhood relations, so that neither a reward function nor a geometric distance needs to be specified. Our experiments show that GCSL-NF overcomes limitations imposed by agents' initial biases, increasingly benefits from negative feedback as learning progresses, and matches or surpasses GCSL- and HER-based methods. By reducing reliance on prespecified reward functions, the proposed approach is particularly relevant for self-adaptive autonomous systems, where adaptation objectives may be diverse, changing, or difficult to engineer.
  </details>

- **[Are Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) Suitable for Imbalanced Data Classification?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.14121)**  `arXiv:2507.14121`  
  _Pankaj Yadav, Vivek Vijay_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) parameterize each connection as a learnable univariate B-spline, offering native feature-level interpretability. Whether this locality helps or hinders under class imbalance, where minority sparsity may leave spline edges without enough local observations to update reliably, remains unexamined. We evaluate KANs against capacity-matched Multilayer Perceptrons (MLPs) and XGBoost across ten imbalanced tabular datasets under three conditions: native class distribution, Focal Loss, and SMOTE-Tomek resampling, within a parameter-parity, two-phase framework. Under the native distribution, KAN spline activations collapse in minority-sparse regions, showing stronger majority-class bias than the matched MLP. Focal Loss yields negligible improvement, as it reweights gradients without providing the localized observations needed for discriminative curvature. Conversely, SMOTE-Tomek resampling lets spline activations recover structured minority-class representations, achieving the best cohort-wide rank and a large, statistically significant gain over unmitigated KANs, though not over resampled baselines. KAN's native spline interpretability directly reveals these dynamics via learned activation profiles, proving representational change rather than threshold recalibration without post-hoc attribution. However, these interpretability gains incur substantially higher training overhead than a parameter-matched MLP across all conditions, with no strategy-dependent latency reduction. Thus, KANs are conditionally suitable for imbalanced tabular classification: effective and interpretable with data-level resampling, yet costly relative to simpler alternatives without it.
  </details>

- **[Symbolic Branch Networks: Tree-Inherited Neural Models for Interpretable Multiclass Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.01781)**  `arXiv:2507.01781`  
  _Dalia Nöth-Rodríguez_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Symbolic Branch Networks (SBNs) are neural models whose architecture is derived directly from an ensemble of decision trees. Each root-to-parent-of-leaf decision path is mapped to a hidden neuron, while the matrices W1 (feature-to-branch) and W2 (branch-to-class) encode the structural relationships induced by the teacher ensemble. This provides an explicit correspondence between teacher branches and neural components, enabling feature-level and branch-level interpretation while retaining the flexibility of gradient-based optimization. The primary configuration studied in this work trains the teacher-derived feature-to-branch matrix W1 through gradient-based learning while keeping the branch-to-class matrix W2 fixed; this configuration is denoted SBN1,0. Across 29 multiclass tabular datasets, this configuration improves upon the teacher ensemble on 28 of 29 datasets, increasing mean accuracy from 84.0% to 87.9%. For reference, XGBoost and TabPFN achieve mean accuracies of 87.3% and 91.3%, respectively, on the same datasets. A one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test on dataset-level mean accuracies indicates a statistically significant improvement of SBN1,0 over the teacher ensemble (p=4.71x10-7). Beyond predictive performance, SBN provides an explicit structural basis for interpretation. Global feature importance can be derived from the teacher-induced feature-to-branch connectivity, while individual predictions can be traced to selected branch-neurons, their associated features, and their class contributions. An analysis across ten independently constructed teacher ensembles shows consistent predictions for a selected instance but only partial stability in its local feature rankings.
  </details>

- **[But what is your honest answer? Aiding LLM-judges with honest alternatives using steering vectors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.17760)**  `arXiv:2505.17760`  
  _Leon Eshuijs, Archie Chaudhury, Alan McBeth, Ethan Nguyen_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  LLM-as-a-judge is widely used as a scalable substitute for human evaluation, yet judges are least reliable on subtle dishonesty such as sycophancy and manipulation, where a judge scoring a response in isolation lacks a reference point. We introduce Judge Using Safety-Steered Alternatives (JUSSA), a framework that reduces this evaluator uncertainty using the assessed model's own internal representations. An honesty-promoting steering vector, optimized from a single training example, generates a contrastive alternative against which each response is judged. On a new manipulation dataset with human-validated response pairs, JUSSA improves AUROC for both GPT-4.1 (0.893$\rightarrow$0.946) and Claude Haiku (0.859$\rightarrow$0.929) judges. The gains concentrate almost entirely on the pairs a judge would otherwise misrank. They reverse once a judge has saturated a task and for the weakest judge we test, so contrastive evaluation helps most when a judge is capable enough to use the reference but has not yet saturated the task. A layer-wise analysis further locates steering effectiveness in the middle layers, where model representations of honest and dishonest prompt processing diverge. Our work demonstrates that steering vectors can serve as tools for evaluation rather than for improving model outputs at inference, opening a new direction for white-box auditing.
  </details>

- **[SPAR: Placement-aware Self-Supervised Representation Learning for Distributed Sensing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.16936)**  `arXiv:2505.16936`  
  _Yizhuo Chen, Tianchen Wang, You Lyu, Yanlan Hu, Jinyang Li, Tomoyoshi Kimura, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  To support distributed sensing applications that require understanding of entities in the environment and their locations, this paper develops a self-supervised approach for placement-aware representation learning in spatially-distributed multi-sensor systems. The goal is to produce a latent representation of the physical environment that decouples upstream sensor placement from downstream analytics (in the sense that the pretrained encoder is reused without retraining when sensor placement changes), while supporting spatial reasoning tasks, such as joint target localization and classification, that are sensitive to sensor placement. A challenge lies in the multiplicity of sensing vantage points that collectively offer information on the shared physical environment. The dependence of measurements on sensor locations implies that the latent representation must jointly encode both the observed signals and observer vantage points, doing so in a way that supports the downstream tasks. Moreover, since the exact deployment-time sensor placement is generally not known at training time, the representation learning framework must be pre-trained to produce such a representation without (training-time) knowledge of deployment-time placement. This challenge distinguishes our goal from approaches, such as NeRF and Gaussian Splatting, that are trained to represent each particular environment given a specific placement of observation points in that environment. In contrast, our representation learning solution, called SPAR, pretrains an encoder independently of future placement by utilizing a novel training objective that emphasizes the duality between signals and vantage points...
  </details>

- **[Simple yet Effective Semi-supervised Knowledge Distillation from Vision-Language Models via Dual-Head Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.07675)**  `arXiv:2505.07675`  
  _Seongjae Kang, Dong Bok Lee, Hyungjoon Jang, Sung Ju Hwang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Semi-supervised learning (SSL) has emerged as a practical solution for addressing data scarcity challenges by leveraging unlabeled data. Recently, vision-language models (VLMs), pre-trained on massive image-text pairs, have demonstrated remarkable zero-/few-shot performance that often surpasses SSL approaches due to their exceptional generalization capabilities. This gap motivates us to question: how can we effectively harness the powerful generalization capabilities of VLMs into task-specific models? Knowledge distillation (KD) offers a natural framework for transferring VLM capabilities, but we identify that it suffers from gradient conflicts between supervised and distillation losses. To address this challenge, we propose Dual-Head Optimization (DHO), which introduces dual prediction heads for each distinct signal. We observe that DHO mitigates gradient conflicts, enabling improved feature learning compared to single-head KD baselines, with practical benefits of minimal computational overhead and test-time hyperparameter tuning without retraining. Extensive experiments across 15 datasets show that DHO consistently outperforms KD baselines, often outperforming teacher models with smaller student models. DHO also achieves new state-of-the-art performance on both in-distribution ImageNet semi-supervised learning and out-of-distribution generalization across ImageNet variants. Code and model checkpoints are publicly available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Local-Order Auxiliary Losses Can Improve Autoencoder Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.04202)**  `arXiv:2504.04202`  
  _Harvey Dam, Martin Burtscher, Tripti Agarwal, Ganesh Gopalakrishnan_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Mean-squared error is the default objective for training autoencoders, yet compressed reconstructions often depend not only on pointwise accuracy but also on preserving local spatial order. We study whether structural auxiliary losses can improve, rather than trade off against, MSE in finite-capacity autoencoders. We introduce finite-difference sign error (FDSE), a local-order auxiliary objective that penalizes disagreements between the signs of neighboring finite differences in the target and reconstruction. FDSE is simple, architecture-agnostic, and differentiable through smooth sign surrogates. Across four tensor reconstruction tasks, we find that moderate mixtures of MSE and FDSE can substantially reduce validation MSE relative to pure MSE training. In coefficient sweeps, FDSE mixtures reduce validation MSE by 2.3$\times$--7.0$\times$ over pure MSE on these tasks, while comparisons with other auxiliary objectives show FDSE to be among the strongest structural objectives tested. The effect is not universal: pure FDSE performs poorly, and gains are largest for coherent spatial fields where local order carries information about the underlying signal. These results suggest that, in compressed-latent reconstruction, appropriately weighted local-structure supervision can guide optimization toward solutions with better pointwise accuracy, rather than merely improving perceptual or structural metrics at MSE's expense.
  </details>

- **[Anomaly Detection via Autoencoder Composite Features and NCE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.01920)**  `arXiv:2502.01920`  
  _Yalin Liao, Austin J. Brockmeier_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Unsupervised anomaly detection is a challenging task. Autoencoders (AEs) or generative models are often employed to model the data distribution of normal inputs and subsequently identify anomalous, out-of-distribution inputs by high reconstruction error or low likelihood, respectively. However, AEs may generalize and achieve small reconstruction errors on abnormal inputs. We propose a decoupled training approach for anomaly detection that both an AE and a likelihood model trained with noise contrastive estimation (NCE). After training the AE, NCE estimates a probability density function, to serve as the anomaly score, on the joint space of the AE's latent representation combined with features of the reconstruction quality. To further reduce the false negative rate in NCE we systematically varying the reconstruction features to augment the training and optimize the contrastive Gaussian noise distribution. Experimental assessments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach matches the performance of prevalent state-of-the-art anomaly detection algorithms.
  </details>

- **[Neural Graph Simulator for Complex Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.09120)**  `arXiv:2411.09120`  
  _Hoyun Choi, Sungyeop Lee, B. Kahng, Junghyo Jo_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Simulating complex systems governed by coupled ordinary differential equations (ODEs) typically requires explicit governing equations and incurs high computational cost from iterative numerical solvers. We propose the Neural Graph Simulator (NGS), a general-purpose data-driven framework that learns multivariate continuous-time dynamics directly from noisy and incomplete observations, without prior knowledge of the equations. Unlike neural ODE-based approaches that depend on repeated solver evaluations, NGS approximates the state transition integral using elapsed time intervals as direct inputs. This eliminates numerical integration while naturally supporting irregular sampling and heterogeneous time scales. Through its graph network architecture, NGS generalizes to unseen graph structures and larger system sizes, as demonstrated on independently sampled Erdős--Rényi graphs. We evaluate NGS on comprehensive benchmarks covering linear diffusion, nonlinear and chaotic dynamics, systems with stiffness-like behavior, and real-world spatiotemporal datasets. NGS combines competitive accuracy across benchmarks with substantial speedups over numerical solvers in computationally demanding settings. Notably, NGS exhibits strong extrapolation to unseen graph sizes and longer time horizons, and supports non-uniform time steps. These results establish NGS as an efficient and scalable alternative to solver-dependent neural simulators.
  </details>

- **[quanda: An Interpretability Toolkit for Training Data Attribution Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.07158)**  `arXiv:2410.07158`  
  _Dilyara Bareeva, Galip Ümit Yolcu, Anna Hedström, Niklas Schmolenski, Thomas Wiegand, Wojciech Samek, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Training data attribution (TDA) methods estimate the influence of individual training samples on a model's predictions, offering a principled lens for interpreting neural networks. Despite rapid methodological progress, TDA evaluation remains scattered across papers and rarely reproducible, making fair comparison between methods challenging. We introduce quanda, a Python toolkit that standardizes TDA evaluation. quanda features a comprehensive collection of evaluation metrics and ready-to-use benchmarks spanning image classification, text classification, and language modeling, alongside a uniform interface for integrating diverse TDA implementations. We showcase quanda through a comparative study of existing TDA methods and find that no approach excels uniformly across metrics, with clear trade-offs between ground-truth faithfulness and downstream task performance. By consolidating the tooling around TDA, quanda equips the community to evaluate attribution methods rigorously and reproducibly. The toolkit is thoroughly tested, documented, and available as an open-source library on PyPI and atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Contextual Causal Bayesian Optimisation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.12412)**  `arXiv:2301.12412`  
  _Vahan Arsenyan, Antoine Grosnit, Haitham Bou-Ammar, Arnak Dalalyan_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We introduce a unified framework for contextual and causal Bayesian optimisation, which aims to design intervention policies maximising the expectation of a target variable. Our approach leverages both observed contextual information and known causal graph structures to guide the search. Within this framework, we propose a novel algorithm that jointly optimises over policies and the sets of variables on which these policies are defined. This thereby extends and unifies two previously distinct approaches: Causal Bayesian Optimisation and Contextual Bayesian Optimisation, while also addressing their limitations in scenarios that yield suboptimal results. We derive worst-case and instance-dependent high-probability regret bounds for our algorithm. We report experimental results across diverse environments, corroborating that our approach achieves sublinear regret and reduces sample complexity in high-dimensional settings.
  </details>

- **[Even Loose Proximity Constraints Make Makespan-optimal Unlabeled Multi-agent Pathfinding Hard](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21277)**  `arXiv:2611.21277`  
  _Takahiro Suzuki, Keisuke Okumura_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We study \textsc{$r$-Connected Unlabeled Multi-agent Pathfinding} ($r$CUMAPF), a variant of MAPF where interchangeable agents have a proximity range $r\in \mathbb{N}$, and agents must form a single group in a given graph $G$ through limited-range communication at all times. The problem arises in fundamental applications such as self-reconfiguration and platooning, while standard MAPF does not capture proximity constraints. For the problem of finding a makespan-optimal solution, prior work shows \NP-hardness for $r=1$ and polynomial-time solvability when $r$ is sufficiently large; the complexity for the intermediate case $2\le r$ is largely unknown. To narrow this gap, we show that finding a solution to $r$CUMAPF with makespan at most $2$ is \NP-hard for $2\le r= O(|V|^{1-\varepsilon})$, where $0<\varepsilon\le 1$ is a fixed constant and $|V|$ is the number of vertices. As a consequence, we show that the labeled analogue of $r$CUMAPF is also \NP-hard under the same condition.
  </details>

- **[Evaluating Authorization and Trust Boundaries in Agentic Orchestration Frameworks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21259)**  `arXiv:2611.21259`  
  _Sahaya Jestus Lazer, Kshitiz Aryal, Maanak Gupta, Elisa Bertino_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Agentic AI systems extend large language models with tools, memory, and multi-agent collaboration, introducing security risks at orchestration boundaries. These risks depend on how identities are represented, operations are authorized, and instructions or information propagate between components. We evaluate LangChain, LangGraph, AutoGen, and OpenClaw through twelve experiments mapped to the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications using a common LLM (gpt-4o-mini). The experiments cover prompt injection, unauthorized resource access and command execution, memory poisoning, and inter-agent trust and identity attacks. Adversarial inputs induced unauthorized tool invocation, while tool chaining, stale filesystem validation, encoded instructions, and inter-agent delegation exposed weaknesses in authorization across component boundaries. Memory poisoning showed that untrusted state can influence responses, a risk distinct from conventional access-control violations. In the evaluated protected configurations, explicit authorization, controlled capability assignment, filesystem containment, and execution safeguards prevented specific unauthorized operations. The findings emphasize preserving authorization and information-trust boundaries throughout agentic workflows rather than treating framework capabilities or model-level instructions as sufficient security guarantees.
  </details>

- **[OpenMAS-GApp: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Domain-Adaptive Multi-Agent Application Construction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20997)**  `arXiv:2611.20997`  
  _Xunkai Li, Kairui Yang, Jiaxi Li, Yuecong Mao, Zekai Chen, Xinle Zhang, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Constructing multi-agent system (MAS) applications across domains requires translating diverse requirements into executable systems, involving task decomposition, agent and tool selection, and execution organization. Existing studies have explored individual aspects of MAS construction, including agent generation, architecture design, workflow generation, and component selection. However, these methods are often developed and evaluated independently, using different task specifications, component resources, and execution settings. This makes it difficult to compare their construction capabilities or determine how they can be applied to different domains. To address this problem, we propose OpenMAS-GApp, a One-for-All benchmark for MAS application construction across diverse domains. It standardizes task inputs, component resources, construction interfaces, and execution environments to support MAS construction under consistent conditions. Within OpenMAS-GApp, we provide Graph Harness as a reference construction method that derives task dependencies, selects compatible agents and tools, and organizes their interactions into executable graphs. We evaluate construction methods across 19 benchmark datasets under 20 evaluation settings spanning four application types and four professional domains.
  </details>

- **[From Vision to Interaction: Evaluating Dynamic Social Intelligence of VLM Agents in ALIVE-World](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20956)**  `arXiv:2611.20956`  
  _Yue Xu, Xiaoyu Qin, Sihan Zhao, Ze-en Xiong, Jia Jia_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  As AI agents are increasingly deployed in real-world applications and take on social roles, dynamic social intelligence, the ability to continuously perceive multimodal cues, infer latent cognitive states, intervene through embodied actions, and ultimately achieve social goals, has become essential. However, existing evaluations largely fragment social intelligence into text-based abstractions, static reasoning tasks, or embodied simulators that lack social dynamics. These approaches fail to capture the multimodal, continuous, and interpersonal complexity of authentic human interactions. To bridge this gap, we introduce ALIVE-World, an embodied simulation environment supporting dynamic multimodal interactions encompassing egocentric vision, language, and non-verbal action. To provide socially grounded interactive feedback, we populate this environment with counterpart agents driven by a profile-conditioned, dual-system (intuitive-affective and logical-cognitive) architecture. Building upon this platform, we propose ALIVE-Bench to transform the assessment of social intelligence into a trackable quantitative framework. By deeply leveraging underlying environmental states and agents' internal variables, ALIVE-Bench systematically evaluates Vision-Language Model (VLM) agents across four critical dimensions: perception, understanding, influence, and outcome. Extensive evaluations reveal that dynamic social intelligence is fundamentally multi-dimensional and scenario-dependent. We identify a critical bottleneck between upstream perception and downstream social intervention, exposing VLM vulnerabilities in fine-grained proxemic awareness, adaptive intervention, and multi-party coordination. By uncovering these limitations and the diverse interaction strategies they produce, this benchmark provides actionable insights for the future behavioral alignment of multimodal agents.
  </details>

- **[When Does Interaction Help? Toward a Reynolds Number for Collective Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20773)**  `arXiv:2611.20773`  
  _Xuening Wu, Haode Yang, Yanlan Kang, Shenqin Yin_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Multi-agent systems combine distributed information through interaction, which can improve performance but also spread errors or suppress useful differences. Predicting when interaction helps is central to understanding and designing collective intelligence. We investigate whether a few dimensionless parameters can predict gains over explicitly defined non-communicating baselines across group sizes, network structures, and tasks, toward a Reynolds-number-like description of collective intelligence. Using distributed classification tasks, stochastic tracking networks, and neural cellular automata, we combine analytical and empirical evidence to examine information sufficiency, dynamical applicability, and finite-sample prediction. We construct inference systems with bounded random variables and matching specified joint moments up to total degree three, yet opposite interaction gains under a fixed readout. These moments alone cannot generally determine the gain sign. Tracking networks likewise exhibit gain reversals despite matched candidate parameters when task power occupies different spectral modes. Under concentrated task spectra and aligned observation noise, however, we derive a low-dimensional similarity relation with an explicit zero-delay error bound and test it across network sizes and topologies under frozen protocols. The relation does not directly apply to the neural cellular systems, where a separate moment-based predictor underperforms direct gain measurement at matched calibration sample budgets. These results establish conditions and limits for low-dimensional gain prediction, providing a restricted similarity law while leaving a general Reynolds-number-like description of collective intelligence open.
  </details>

- **[World-Model-Guided Plan Search for Cooperative Mixed-Traffic Control at Bottlenecks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20067)**  `arXiv:2611.20067`  
  _Jinghan Peng, Ning Liu, Xiangrui Kong, Sen Shen, Dongkun Han_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Across 192 paired test scenarios at 60% penetration and a demand of 2,800 vehicles per hour, the searched library reduces mean total delay by 14.3% relative to MAPPO and by 3.8% relative to a handwritten plan library. The largest increase in group mean delay is 6.2 s, below the prescribed 10 s limit. In a separate screening experiment, the guided search achieves a 30.0% pass rate compared with 2.6% for random sampling.   </details>

- **[Delay-Aware Reinforcement Learning for O-RAN Control under Stochastic Reward Feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19344)**  `arXiv:2611.19344`  
  _Xingqi Wu, Junaid Farooq, Tao Li, Juntao Chen, Ying Wang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Reinforcement learning (RL) is increasingly employed for real-time control in Open Radio Access Networks (O-RANs). However, the asynchronous nature of O-RAN feedback introduces stochastic delays between actions and their observable rewards, leading to misaligned credit assignment and unstable training. This letter formulates the O-RAN control problem as a Markov decision process (MDP) with delayed and stochastic rewards, where the true reward corresponding to an action is received after an unknown delay. To address this, we propose a delay-aware deep RL framework that integrates a long short-term memory (LSTM)-based delay predictor and a temporal reward realignment module within an off-policy learning pipeline. Using empirical delay traces collected from the Open AI Cellular (OAIC) testbed, we demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves faster convergence and significantly reduces latency violations and packet drops compared to conventional RL methods that ignore feedback delay. The results confirm that reward-delay compensation is critical for reliable AI-driven O-RAN control.
  </details>

- **[When Reviews Gate Access: Collusion, Sabotage and the Scale of Peer Review in the AI Submission Surge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19054)**  `arXiv:2611.19054`  
  _Yuchen Li, Xintong Li, Ken-Tye Yong, Nguyen H. Tran_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  AI tools have helped push submissions to the largest machine-learning venues to tens of thousands per cycle. Venues have answered with rules that tie access to review: per-author caps, mandatory reciprocal reviewing, reviewer eligibility earned through accepted papers, and assignment based on reviewer bids. Under these rules a reviewer is also a competitor of the authors. We study two deviations that the rules make attractive. Sabotage lowers a competitor's score. Collusion raises an ally's score. We build an agent-based conference calibrated to public statistics of NeurIPS and ICLR and run 6,220 simulated conferences. Four results stand out. First, the two deviations do different harm and amplify each other. Collusion changes who is accepted, sabotage erodes what scores say about quality, and rings that may also sabotage gain more than rings that only collude. Second, under random assignment the chance that collusion changes a decision is set by one exposure index, $E = Rm/A$, the expected number of allies among a paper's reviewers. Growth therefore protects random assignment, but bidding removes the protection. In a pool of 3,000 reviewers a 20-member ring turns 0.8% of its papers into acceptances under random assignment and 71% when 30% of allies' bids are granted. Third, when agents choose their allies every cycle, caps at the inner layers of the social brain keep collusion nearly harmless. Without a cap agents ally with half of their area and accepted value falls by 35%. Fourth, reviewer eligibility tied to acceptances turns sabotage into a weapon of incumbents, and a longer eligibility window widens the gap between incumbents and newcomers only when sabotage is possible.
  </details>

- **[CANDO: Cooperative Agentic Network for Layout Design Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10044)**  `arXiv:2610.10044`  
  _Athanasios Masouris, Zheng Jing, Benjamin Sam Chandler, Hadi Jamali-Rad_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Layout generation for real-world facilities is a challenging problem, requiring reasoning over irregular site boundaries, heterogeneous orientations, access-aware placements, and motion-planning feasibility. Motivated by these gaps, we introduce ALPS-Bench, a benchmark of $1,000$ professionally annotated real-world facility layouts paired with an instance-specific scoring protocol grounded in a structured design manual. As a strong baseline for ALPS-Bench, we propose CANDO, a training-free multi-agent framework in which specialized agents iteratively refine layouts through a verification-grounded loop, concentrating reasoning on strategic spatial decisions. We demonstrate that CANDO surpasses state-of-the-art trained and LLM-based baselines on the widely adopted PubLayNet, RICO, and PKU-PosterLayout benchmarks, establishing cooperative agentic design as a broadly effective recipe for constraint-aware layout synthesis. Code and benchmark are available through our project page:this https URL
  </details>

- **[Do Multi-Agent LLMs Explore Each Other?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11250)**  `arXiv:2607.11250`  
  _Hyeong Kyu Choi, Jiatong Li, Wendi Li, Xin Eric Wang, Sharon Li_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Exploration is essential for reliable autonomy in multi-agent systems, yet it remains unclear whether large language model (LLM) agents can explore effectively when interacting with one another. We show that modern LLM agents often fail to do so, exhibiting myopic and polarized interaction patterns that lead to suboptimal coordination and increased regret. We formalize this challenge as the Multi-Agent Exploration problem, modeling it as a partially observable stochastic game (POSG), in which agents must probe peers to infer their capabilities and identify effective interaction strategies. To address this, we introduce Multi-Agent Contextual Exploration (MACE), a lightweight framework that explicitly promotes exploration through structured peer selection. Across both contextual and parametric diversity settings, exploration behavior and downstream task performance substantially improve when MACE is applied.   </details>

- **[ScaleVLA: Scaling Vision-Language-Action Models to 552 Billion Parameters](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21607)**  `arXiv:2611.21607`  
  _Ruixi Yu, Dairu Liu, Xuchuan Chen, Zekun Qi, Zekai Li, Zhuo Cao, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Frontier Vision-Language Models (VLMs) such as GPT-6 Astra have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in robot control, suggesting that broad pretraining provides knowledge valuable for physical action. Yet most Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies still rely on much smaller VLM backbones, leaving this potential largely untapped. We ask whether frontier-scale representations can provide a stronger foundation for robot learning. We introduce ScaleVLA, which connects a 552B DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash backbone to a trainable action DiT, and systematically compare VLMs from 2B to 552B under a shared training setup. We evaluate three fundamental capabilities of robot foundation models. In sample efficiency, just 10 demonstrations outperform a 2B backbone trained with 50 (87.8% vs. 85.6%). In generalization, LIBERO-PRO success reaches 45.1%, compared with at most 31.3% for smaller backbones. In precise manipulation, real-world charger insertion improves from 4/10 to 9/10 successes, with gains concentrated in contact-sensitive alignment. Despite its scale, ScaleVLA achieves 216 ms median latency per action chunk. Our findings suggest that frontier VLMs can serve not only as reasoning agents, but also as powerful representational foundations for efficient and generalizable robot policies.
  </details>

- **[SADL: On the Demand-Supply Geometry of Representation Collapse](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21596)**  `arXiv:2611.21596`  
  _Junhan Sun, Yigui Feng, Mingzhe Liu, Haoyan Xu, Lei Ye, Ziqi Han, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  In Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs), a well-constrained projector output does not by itself prevent representation collapse. We find that, from initialization, the encoder representation is dominated by a component shared by different inputs. A batch-normalized projector removes this component, so regularization after the projector cannot correct it, and the differences between representations shrink until they collapse. We propose SADL (Supply And Demand Loss), which keeps the original training objective and constrains the encoder directly when needed. SADL compares the representation differences that the projector output demands with the differences the encoder can retain and pass on to the projector, and adds a constraint on the encoder only when supply falls short of demand. It works with different Demand Regularizers and introduces no auxiliary networks, additional trainable parameters, or architectural changes. In single-task and jointly trained four-task LeWorldModel (LeWM) and INTACT experiments, SADL lowers the collapse rate over ten random seeds from 50% to 0%. After one epoch of training, encoder effective rank is 3.4-6.4 times that of the corresponding baseline without SADL, and latent prediction error falls to 1/20-1/303 of it. Without additional tuning, SADL stays robust as its loss weight spans orders of magnitude, and with several Demand Regularizers INTACT exceeds 95% mean search-free control success. On four image datasets, SADL also consistently improves accuracy and stability across random seeds. These results show that matching the representation differences a regularizer demands with the differences the encoder can supply leads to faster and more stable representation learning in control and image classification.
  </details>

- **[Lazy-MOSAIC: Accelerating Skill-Centric Manipulation Planning with Learned Skill-Effect World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21517)**  `arXiv:2611.21517`  
  _Itamar Mishani, Mukund Krishnakumar, Oren Salzman, Maxim Likhachev_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Long-horizon manipulation tasks require a robot to perform a sequence of physical interactions with its environment, typically combining several different skills. Planning such behaviors efficiently is challenging: given a library of parameterized skills, solutions lie in a vast hybrid space of skill sequences and their parameters, and evaluating each candidate skill's feasibility and effect with a high-fidelity world model such as a physics simulator is computationally expensive. MOSAIC, a recent skill-centric approach, lets the skills guide a non-sequential search toward the regions of this space where they are likely to succeed; however, it pays the full cost of simulation for every parameterized skill it considers. In this work, we introduce Lazy-MOSAIC, a lazy planning framework that instead searches over hypothesized skill outcomes. A cheap learned skill-effect world model predicts, in a fraction of a millisecond, a skill's feasibility and the world state it produces. Lazy-MOSAIC then uses these predictions to focus expensive simulation on promising candidate skills and, when a hypothesis is invalidated, repairs only the affected part of the search, while ensuring that every skill in a returned plan is validated in simulation. We evaluate Lazy-MOSAIC on cluttered-shelf retrieval tasks of increasing difficulty and demonstrate it on a physical robot, showing that it plans substantially faster than baselines with fewer simulator queries, while matching or exceeding their success rate in every setting. Visitthis http URL.
  </details>

- **[GHySSeg: Real-Time Geometric Ground and Road Segmentation for Hybrid Solid-State LiDAR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21507)**  `arXiv:2611.21507`  
  _Martín Palos, Fernando García_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Hybrid solid-state LiDAR sensors are making their way into production vehicles, yet the data they produce differs structurally from that of the established spinning mechanical sensors behind today's autonomous-driving datasets: it is ring-free, dense, cluttered, and concentrated in a frontal field of view. The classical geometric methods that autonomous vehicles rely on for drivable space computation and navigation assume the ordered ring-and-column structure of a 360-degree spinning LiDAR and degrade or fail on this data, while learned alternatives are computationally heavy, hard to certify, and trained almost exclusively on spinning-LiDAR data. We demonstrate that the same dense, per-curve geometry is instead an opportunity to close the divide between the industry's preferred sensors and autonomous-driving research. We present GHySSeg, a purely geometric method that segments ground and drivable road from a single hybrid solid-state LiDAR frame by tracing each scan curve and reading two geometric signatures, a step in height and a fold-back in range, with no training and no graphics processing unit. To evaluate it, we release HySoLiD-Drive, the first public benchmark dedicated to ground and road segmentation on an automotive hybrid solid-state LiDAR, comprising 100 manually labeled and 7000 unlabeled frames recorded by two vehicles in real driving. On this benchmark, GHySSeg surpasses both geometric and learned state-of-the-art baselines across ground and road segmentation, reaching an intersection-over-union of 0.907 for road and 0.896 for ground at over 0.96 precision, while running in real time at about 22 milliseconds per frame on a single core.
  </details>

- **[Safe Physical Interaction of All-Electric Heavy-Duty Robotic Manipulators via Control Barrier Functions and Variable Impedance Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21309)**  `arXiv:2611.21309`  
  _Amir Hossein Barjini, Mohammad Bahari, Jouni Mattila_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  All-electric heavy-duty robotic manipulators are increasingly expected to operate close to tunnel walls, equipment, and other structures while retaining the force capability required for large-payload tasks. Accurate motion control alone does not address the resulting safety and interaction requirements. This paper develops a safety-aware physical-interaction architecture that combines variable impedance control (VIC) with control barrier functions (CBFs) on top of an established virtual decomposition control (VDC) framework for electromechanical linear actuator (EMLA)-driven manipulators. VIC continuously adapts the task-space stiffness and damping according to predicted proximity and contact risk, whereas a joint-velocity CBF filter enforces Cartesian workspace boundaries and the physical stroke limits induced by the closed-chain lift and tilt mechanisms. To account for nonideal realization of the filtered velocity by the inner VDC/EMLA dynamics, the CBF inequalities are tightened using a measured bound on the joint-velocity tracking error. Four configurations, namely VDC, VIC+VDC, CBF+VDC, and VIC+CBF+VDC, are evaluated under workspace, actuator-limit, and physical-interaction scenarios. VIC reduces the peak and RMS environment-interaction forces by 92.59% and 96.33%, respectively; both robust CBF configurations maintain positive workspace and EMLA safety margins, while VIC+CBF+VDC reduces the CBF intervention metric by 10.30% compared with CBF+VDC.
  </details>

- **[ThinkWAM: Rethinking Latent Futures for Action Refinement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21258)**  `arXiv:2611.21258`  
  _Haoyun Tang, Baqiao Deng, Enjin Zhou, Songwen Tian, Keyao Xu, Bowen Jing, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  World-action models (WAMs) couple action generation with predictions of future states. An initial action chunk may be flawed. A future prediction that is not conditioned on the chunk may fail to reflect the changes that the proposed actions would induce in visual representations, limiting its usefulness for refinement before execution. We introduce ThinkWAM, a latent WAM that establishes bidirectional feedback before execution through a proposal-rethink-refine loop: the policy first proposes a complete action chunk, the proposal corrects multi-horizon future latents through a learned residual, and the corrected latents are injected into a second pass of the same action head, which generates the executable chunk. An affordance-guided observation-action memory and a near-fine, far-coarse multi-horizon prediction scheme, both motivated by predictive coding, support this loop, and all prediction stays in latent space. ThinkWAM achieves 64.4% mean success across three real-world OOD conditions. The mean two-pass inference latency per action chunk is 153.48 ms on LIBERO, 164.61 ms on RoboTwin, and 101.2 ms on the Galaxea A1Z. Ablations show complementary gains from rethinking and affordance guidance. Diagnostics indicate that proposal-conditioned corrections change both predicted futures and action trajectories, showing that the corrected future representations improve the final action.
  </details>

- **[Cooperative Mobile Manipulation using Learned Dynamical Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21198)**  `arXiv:2611.21198`  
  _Saray Bakker, Wendelin Böhmer, Javier Alonso-Mora_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Cooperative mobile manipulation requires robots to coordinate their motions while ensuring whole-body collision avoidance and preserving task-relevant behaviors. - **[Polygraph: Large-Scale Multi-Session Trajectory Optimization using Pose Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21163)**  `arXiv:2611.21163`  
  _Petar Lukovic, Tian Yi Lim, Marc Pollefeys, Pablo Speciale, Hermann Blum, Zuria Bauer_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Robots, vehicles, and wearable devices often traverse the same environment many times. Each pass produces its own trajectory from onboard visual or visual-inertial odometry. These trajectories are locally accurate but drift over time and live in unrelated coordinate frames. Turning many such independent trajectories into one globally consistent set is the large-scale multi-session trajectory optimization problem. Existing solutions largely work offline. All sessions must be available up front, one session is fixed as the reference frame, and a single fused map is then optimized. This paper presents Polygraph, a multi-session trajectory optimization pipeline that processes sessions online, one keyframe and one spatial cluster at a time, and never builds a 3D map. Keyframes are grouped into local clusters. When a cluster closes, it is matched against every other session through learned image retrieval. Candidate pairs are verified with sparse feature matching, monocular metric depth, and robust pose estimation. A two-tier consensus gate admits a cross-session edge into the shared pose graph only once independent evidence corroborates it. A cheap incremental solve keeps the graph current, and a periodic robust batch solve prunes outliers. We evaluate Polygraph on stereo outdoor driving, HoloLens and iPad indoor traversals, legged indoor locomotion with a Boston Dynamics Spot, and large-scale outdoor vehicle and handheld routes. Against the closest prior work on the same GPU model, using its reported timings, Polygraph runs faster, commits fewer loop-closure edges, and matches or improves on accuracy.
  </details>

- **[WinDEX: Metric 3D Hand Motion Reconstruction in the Wild for Dexterous Teleoperation and Policy Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21143)**  `arXiv:2611.21143`

- **[Linglong Agent Service: A Runtime for Centralized Agent Reasoning and Distributed Execution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21129)**  `arXiv:2611.21129`

  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We further present online_debugger as the process-scale special case of execution-site separation: an instrumented program submits exception evidence, executes session-scoped inspection tools inside the incident process, and resumes the same diagnostic session.   </details>

- **[ReuseMem: One Memory, Multiple Goals in Robot Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21115)**  `arXiv:2611.21115`  
  _Yoonseok Kang, Dayeon Jung, Seunghoon Jeon, Wonjib Kim, Dongchul Park_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Robots that work alongside people should be able to use what they have seen when new requests arise. - **[ForceHarness: Turning Force into Action and Physics for Frozen Frontier Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21099)**  `arXiv:2611.21099`  
  _Ke Sun, Kevin Yuchen Ma, Yike Zhang, Yanzhe Chen, Mike Zheng Shou_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Frontier multimodal models can now control robots zero-shot from images, yet many manipulation tasks depend on contact forces that images cannot show. Bringing force to an API-only frozen model raises two challenges. First, contact evolves much faster than an API model can decide, so the system must close the loop on force beneath the model. In simulation, it adds 17.5 percentage points on the public ForceBench suite and 34.3 percentage points on HiddenPhys, surpassing force-aware policies trained on demonstrations on both benchmarks and matching hand-written expert controllers on HiddenPhys.   </details>

- **[CoopDistill: Equilibrium-Guided Multi-Agent Policy Distillation for Cooperative Driving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21069)**  `arXiv:2611.21069`  
  _Shiyu Fang, Sheng Zhao, Jiarui Zhang, Chengkai Xu, Xiaocong Zhao, Peng Hang, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Cooperative driving extends autonomous driving from individual vehicle decisions to joint maneuvers that improve traffic safety and efficiency. Optimization-based methods impose safety constraints but often fix paths to simplify multi-vehicle planning, limiting spatial flexibility. Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) explores alternatives through interaction, but coordinated learning and safe execution remain challenging. Their integration nevertheless faces challenges in exploration efficiency, experience allocation, and execution reliability. To address these challenges, this paper proposes CoopDistill, an equilibrium-guided multi-agent policy distillation framework. A potential-game (PG) formulation provides a fixed-path longitudinal reference, around which a residual MARL policy learns longitudinal acceleration, conflict-approach timing, and lateral path corrections. A comparative rollout selector evaluates the joint consequences of learned corrections against PG before choosing the executed action. Experiments in merging, roundabout, and intersection scenarios compare CoopDistill with six baselines at four connected automated vehicle penetration levels. Relative to PG, success improves by 2.1--27.1 percentage points and delay decreases by 7.3--27.3\%, with no observed collisions. Code is available atthis https URL
  </details>

- **[Multi-CONDOR: Learning Multistable Motion Primitives from Demonstration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21059)**  `arXiv:2611.21059`  
  _Gabriele Giuseppe Di Marzo, Mariano Ramírez Montero, Maximilian Stölzle, Rodrigo Pérez-Dattari, Cosimo Della Santina_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Dynamical-system-based motion policies provide a framework for learning reactive robot motions with stability and convergence properties. Many manipulation tasks, however, admit several distinct goals or a continuous set of acceptable outcomes, requiring motion primitives that preserve these alternatives. Accommodating both goal structures within a unified framework with continuous, autonomous dynamics remains an open challenge. We propose a CONDOR-based framework, multi-CONDOR, for learning motion primitives with either multiple discrete attractors or a continuous attracting goal contour. The approach combines imitation learning with losses that encourage agreement between the learned task dynamics and latent reference systems encoding the desired attraction structure. We provide a Lyapunov-based analysis of the convergence properties of the learned motion dynamics. We evaluate the framework on simulated benchmarks with discrete goals, qualitative examples with continuous goal contours, and robotic grasping experiments. In simulation, multi-CONDOR reduces trajectory RMSE by approximately 72% compared with separately learned single-goal motion primitives selected by a state machine. For tasks with two and three goals, respectively, it reduces the fraction of evaluated initial states ending outside the goal tolerance from StableNODE's 0.31% and 7.29% to 0% in both settings. Experiments with a Franka Emika robot arm demonstrate successful grasping of a container by either of its two handles using motions learned from demonstrations. Together, these results show multi-CONDOR combines motion reproduction with the flexibility to converge to alternative valid outcomes.
  </details>

- **[WiTac: Wrist-Informed Tactile Representations for Contact-Rich Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21057)**  `arXiv:2611.21057`  
  _Haotian He, Yiyang Chen, Congsheng Xu, Wenchao Yue, Mingze Ye, Shuai Chen, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Similar tactile contacts can call for different corrections depending on the configuration of the hand, object and target. Rather than supplying touch and wrist vision separately, fusing them before policy injection better grounds tactile features in visual context, yielding more accurate contact representations. We introduce Wrist-Informed Tactile Representations (WiTac), a pretrained encoder that learns such representations before action generation. Pretrained on nearly 300 hours of SharpaDex data, WiTac deeply fuses tactile signals with hand motion and wrist views into a comprehensive contact representation. Conditioning downstream VLA policies (GR00T N1.7 and $\pi_{0.5}$) on WiTac substantially improves task success over vision-only base policies across four contact-rich manipulation tasks (+28.8% and +15.0% on average), and further outperforms a wrist-free tactile encoder by 18.8% and 7.5%, respectively. Offline analyses further show that incorporating wrist vision yields more accurate contact descriptors, stronger joint task-contact discrimination, greater feature stability under tactile noise, and clearer action-direction readout from similarthis http URLpage:this https URL.
  </details>

- **[FlowRow: Learning Navigation Behaviors in Agricultural Environments with Long-Horizon Goal-Conditioned Flow Matching Policies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21035)**  `arXiv:2611.21035`  
  _Utkarsh Bajpai, Cédric Pradalier, Stéphanie Aravecchia_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Autonomous monitoring and intervention in semi-structured agricultural environments, such as orchards and vineyards, require mobile robots to navigate to locations across diverse field configurations. This entails performing navigation behaviors including in-row driving, row turning and skipping, and inter-row traversal. Recent learning-based approaches have enabled robust in-row navigation from onboard perception, but navigation across rows typically requires a priori knowledge of field geometry to specify and tune row-transition maneuvers, preventing arbitrary transitions between rows. We address this challenge by framing navigation in these environments as a goal-directed navigation task, where a long-horizon goal is expressed relative to the robot and a planner generates local paths based on the goal and the robot's perceptual observations. We present FlowRow, a flow-matching-based local planner which models the distribution of diverse agricultural navigation behaviors as $\mathrm{SE}(2)$ paths using the long-horizon goal and depth perception. To enable systematic evaluation, we introduce RowNavBench, a navigation benchmark for semi-structured agricultural environments developed in Isaac Sim, comprising 900 episodes across grape vineyards, lemon orchards, and apple orchards with varying row lengths, row and plant spacings, plant positions, and weed growth. FlowRow achieves 87% success, compared to 44% for the strongest generative behavior cloning baseline retrained on the same demonstrations. We will release our benchmark, data, and code upon acceptance.
  </details>

- **[Inverse Kinematics in Endoscopic Scenarios using MoveIt](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20978)**  `arXiv:2611.20978`  
  _Marc Bestmann, Timon Engelke, Rebecca Rodeck, Gerko Wende_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Inverse kinematics are critical in many robotic applications, yet standard MoveIt-based solvers struggle in confined scenarios. This paper provides a benchmark of the available solvers and compares multiple practical modifications for improving the performance of the solvers. Splitting the IK problem into two parts results in the best performance, leading to a 100% success rate under 100 ms in an endoscopic tank scenario.
  </details>

- **[ROSE: A Shared Cross-Embodiment Facial-Motion Latent Space for Humanoid Robot Expression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20950)**  `arXiv:2611.20950`  
  _Yongji Fu, Man Cao, Yi Zhou, Fei Lin, Mark F. Hansen, Guanqun Cao_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Natural, coherent full-face dynamic expressions are central to making humanoid robots socially approachable, yet existing systems commonly realize only limited lip motion or scripted expressions. The limitation is both physical and algorithmic. A compact head leaves little room for densely packed, independently controllable actuation; meanwhile, learned systems often generate an avatar video, landmarks, or facial parameters and then infer actuator commands through visual retargeting. This render-and-invert path adds latency and artifacts, and it does not reliably transfer generated behavior to a physical robot. We present ROSE (RObot facial expression through Shared motion Embeddings), a framework that integrates biomimetic hardware, cross-embodiment motion representation learning, and multimodal motion generation. On the hardware side, we build a flexible tendon-sheath transmission structure that integrates 34 actuators into a 19.5 cm biomimetic head. By decoupling actuator placement from facial action points, it enables coordinated full-face expression within a compact volume. On the algorithmic side, ROSE-VAE learns an identity-independent shared facial-motion latent space from human, digital-human, and robot observations. ROSE-Flow directly maps text, audio, or their combination to trajectories in this motion space without using video as a generator input. ROSE-ACT then converts these trajectories into constrained actuator commands. Our system demonstrates how high-density biomimetic hardware and a shared executable facial-motion representation can jointly unify cross-embodiment learning, multimodal generation, and physical robot expression.
  </details>

- **[TacBridge: Learning Unified Tactile Representations through Cross-Sensor Correspondence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20939)**  `arXiv:2611.20939`  
  _Yongji Fu, Yijiong Lin, Yi Zhou, Yi Qi, Guanqun Cao_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Optical tactile sensors record tactile videos that capture local deformation and its temporal evolution during contact, supporting robot manipulation, force estimation, and tactile representation learning. Differences in imaging geometry, background appearance, illumination, resolution, and deformation response lead to sensor-dependent observations of the same contact across GelSight, DIGIT, GelSlim, TacTip, and other optical tactile sensors. This variability limits representation transfer and the joint use of multi-sensor data. We introduce TacBridge, a framework for learning unified representations from multi-sensor tactile videos through cross-sensor correspondence. Specifically, multi-sensor masked tactile-video pre-training learns spatiotemporal representations across sensors. We then train the same masked model jointly on same-sensor and cross-sensor reconstruction, using paired source and target videos of matched contact events. Experiments on cross-sensor translation and downstream perception demonstrate the cross-sensor generalization and task transferability of the learned tactile representations.
  </details>

- **[Driving the Style: Velocity-Conditioned Whole-Body Control from Motion Demonstrations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20888)**  `arXiv:2611.20888`  
  _Murad Dawood, Oezge Drama Berkenkamp, Antonio Gonzales Marin, Nutan Chen_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Achieving human-like behavior on humanoid robots has advanced rapidly by leveraging motion-capture demonstrations rather than hand-crafted cost functions. Adversarial imitation supplies a style signal that lets a policy fulfill a task while adhering to a desired style, but is difficult to transfer to hardware. Whole-body tracking through reinforcement learning instead deploys reliably and imitates demonstrations faithfully, but the resulting policies are conditioned on the future reference, so they require a reference trajectory at runtime and can fail when the motion differs from the training data. We train a humanoid policy directly with whole-body tracking rewards while restricting its actor to compact locomotion commands and robot observations. Reference motion supervises the reward and privileged critic, without supplying reference joint trajectories to the actor or requiring teacher distillation. The demonstrated style is thereby encoded in the policy through the tracking reward, so the robot reproduces the whole-body style under commanded velocities. Trained on a single random-walk motion and commanded with velocity profiles from held-out motions, our policy reaches at least 98\% success in simulation and completes every trial on the Unitree G1. On held-out slow walking, whole-body tracking drops to 2\% success and command-conditioned distillation to 56\%, and both fail on the real robot. On the trained motions, the joint position error of our policy stays within 8\% of whole-body tracking, and it has a higher style coverage than adversarial motion priors (AMP), which fell on the real robot without a safety crane.
  </details>

- **[QTOP: Scaling Humanoid Motion Tracking with Quantile Critics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20791)**  `arXiv:2611.20791`  
  _Markus Peschl, Dana Kianfar, Daniel Dijkman_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Learning human motion tracking policies through reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a core capability that underpins a majority of recent progress in humanoid whole-body control. However, achieving generalization to unseen motions at high fidelity requires jointly scaling training to thousands of GPU and dataset hours. This work hypothesizes that motion tracking is inherently compute-bound because training on a diverse set of motions introduces learning interference, similar to multi-task RL. To tackle this, we propose Quantile Tracking Optimization (QTOP), which improves sample efficiency by introducing a distributional advantage estimate conditioned on state and reference pairs.
