  </details>

- **[MOSU2: Long-range Navigation System with Multi-modal Scene Understanding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11148)**  `arXiv:2611.11148`  
  _Jing Liang, Zhenyu Hou, Senthurbavan Kirubaharan, Md Safwan Mondal, Ashok Gudivada, Xuesu Xiao, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Robots that travel long distances through public outdoor spaces must do more than avoid obstacles: they must remain on terrain suited to their mobility and decide when to proceed, yield, or detour around pedestrians, cyclists, vehicles, traffic signals, and temporary restrictions. These decisions are difficult because their correctness often depends on how a scene evolves, such as whether an approaching car is slowing or a cyclist will cross the robot's path. Vision-language models (VLMs) can interpret such cues, but they reason over images that lack metric geometry and motion. Supplying this evidence at every step is too slow for real-time navigation, and hand-crafted triggers cannot anticipate the open-ended variety of outdoor situations. We present MOSU2, a long-range navigation system with two-stage trajectory selection, in which first-stage contextual reasoning determines when additional evidence is needed and what to retrieve. Only when an interaction remains unresolved does the first stage trigger the second stage to retrieve geometric and dynamic information and align it with scene context to make navigation decisions. Building on MOSU, MOSU2 follows routes from GPS-based route planning and filters candidate trajectories through multi-modal traversability analysis before selecting a trajectory to move the robot. In real-world experiments spanning stop gestures, construction sites, crosswalks, and roads shared with vehicles, cyclists, and pedestrians, MOSU2 raises mean navigation success from 61.8% to 94.2% and condition-detection accuracy from 72.2% to 91.4% over its single-image predecessor, at about 2.2 times its mean decision latency. Project website:this https URL
  </details>

- **[Data-Driven Configuration of Protective Separation Zones in Collaborative Robot Cells from Operator Occupancy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07621)**  `arXiv:2611.07621`  
  _Aulon Bajrami, Theo Jacobs, Werner Kraus_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  The protective separation zone of a collaborative robot cell is commonly dimensioned for a worst case that disregards where the operator is actually present during the task. This paper presents a camera-based, data-driven method that configures this zone from observed operator occupancy. Operator positions accumulated over several production shifts are aggregated into an occupancy heatmap, from which a protective field is derived that trades off the achievable robot velocity against the required safety distance, following the speed and separation monitoring principle of ISO/TS 15066. The resulting configuration is advisory, that is, reviewed within the risk assessment rather than applied autonomously to the robot controller. The method, which builds on a pose-based perception pipeline with activity recognition, was evaluated in two operational cells at two industrial partners, where the protective field could be reduced by approximately 17% and a productivity increase of 9% was measured. However, adoption proved to depend on more than the demonstrated gain alone.
  </details>

- **[VLALagBench: Understanding When and Why VLA Inference Latency Matters](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03103)**  `arXiv:2611.03103`  
  _Qi Wen, Borui Xu, Hussein Amro, Hongshi Tan, Hanmin Lin, Chaoyi Ruan, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Vision-language-action (VLA) models offer a promising path toward general-purpose robot manipulation. While inference latency can affect task success in a constantly evolving physical world, the relationship between latency and task success rate remains poorly understood. In this paper, we introduce VLALagBench, a comprehensive benchmark for studying VLA inference latency sensitivity across task types, object speeds, execution modes (synchronous and asynchronous), and VLA policies. Using VLALagBench, we find that even a modest inference latency of 100 ms can nearly halve task success on moving targets, with sensitivity varying substantially across tasks and policies. These differences reflect task-specific requirements for precision and continuous motion. By overlapping inference with action execution, asynchronous execution can recover some of the lost success at the cost of more frequent inference requests. Building on these findings, we develop an empirical model that predicts task success from limited calibration data, achieving root-mean-square prediction errors of only 5.7-7.8% across various VLA policies. Given an inference system's latency and per-robot throughput, these predictions guide the selection of system-specific VLA algorithm configurations to maximize task success. We believe VLALagBench and these findings provide a solid foundation for future robotics algorithm-system co-design.
  </details>

- **[Veloxity: Towards Memory-Safe UAV Embedded Firmware using the Rust Programming Language](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.41053)**  `arXiv:2610.41053`  
  _Derek Ward, Brian Bascom, Tyler Larsen, James Usevitch, Phil Tokumaru, Tim McLain_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Recent years have witnessed increased momentum towards memory-safe programming languages for safety-critical systems. Memory-safe languages can eliminate entire classes of common software errors that have historically required extensive analysis and expenditure to avoid. Nevertheless, memory-safe language adoption in aerospace remains fragmented and incomplete, particularly for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). Recent Rust UAV projects either run only in simulation, are closed source, or have not been integrated with an established autonomy ecosystem and tested against existing C/C++ firmware. To address this gap, we present Veloxity: an open-source embedded UAV autopilot written in the memory-safe Rust programming language. Veloxity lowers the barrier to using memory-safe languages within modern ecosystems by providing a minimal, modular foundation for autonomous UAVs. We compare Veloxity to equivalent autopilots written in C++ in simulation, with hardware testbenches, and via outdoor waypoint-following flight tests, demonstrating functional parity with improved performance. These results indicate that modern memory-safe languages are a viable option for reliable and performant firmware for autonomous aerospace systems.
  </details>

- **[Actuator-Aware Observer Inputs for Cascade ADRC of Quadrotors Under Rotor Lag, Measurement Delay and Sensor Noise](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.39126)**  `arXiv:2610.39126`  
  _Xuan-Quy Dao, Ngoc-Bich Le, Le-Minh Nguyen_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  In sampled cascade linear active disturbance rejection control (LADRC) of quadrotors, the extended-state observer is usually driven by the instantaneous command, although the delayed measurement reflects an earlier, rotor-filtered acceleration. This simulation and software-in-the-loop (SITL) study examines actuator-aware (AA) observer inputs: the altitude and attitude observers use the limited virtual input filtered by a rotor-lag model and aligned with the measurement delay, and the horizontal observers use the acceleration reconstructed from the measured attitude. Fixed gains are selected on the sampled model under sensitivity and step-response requirements and covariance-based ceilings on the noise-induced control increment, including the path from position noise to the inner loop. In 30 paired set-point trials, the two AA designs reach position root-mean-square errors (RMSEs) of 19.2 and 16.9~mm, versus 65.5~mm for a proportional-integral-derivative (PID) controller tuned under the same requirements, with lower rotor-command increments. Ablations attribute the improvement to the rotor-lag model and the measured-attitude input; delay alignment is negligible at the nominal 5-ms delay. PX4 SITL runs reproduce these results within 2~mm. Behind the PX4 state estimator, the white-noise ceilings no longer describe the loop. After redesign with an identified estimation-error model, one AA design reduces the set-point RMSE from 59.1 to 44.0~mm with a 15\% lower quantized rotor-command increment, whereas the half-gain variant is worse than the PID. With fixed gains, the AA designs tolerate less unmodelled rotor lag and delay than the PID. Hardware validation remains future work.
  </details>

- **[Ego-CEVR: Learning Cross-Embodiment Visual Representations from Human Egocentric Videos](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37509)**  `arXiv:2610.37509`  
  _Keru Zhou, Zhirui Fang, Xinrun Xu, Yaopeng Lou, Zeyuan He, Zihao Zhu, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Egocentric videos offer a low-cost, scalable source of manipulation experience for robot learning. However, existing methods often fail to tailor their use of egocentric videos and robot demonstrations to the differences in their formats and information content. We present Ego-CEVR, a data-native framework for hierarchical visual representation learning that assigns distinct learning objectives to global and interaction representations. The global module learns task context through future video prediction, while the interaction module uses this context to interpret wrist observations and learns local execution information through robot action supervision. The distinct learning objectives enable independent pretraining on large-scale human and robot egocentric videos to learn task context, and training on real-robot demonstrations to align the learned representations with fine-grained robot actions. Experiments show leading performance on LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin 2.0, while real-robot evaluations demonstrate generalization across tasks and embodiments.
  </details>

- **[How Tuning, Reference Preview, Actuator Modeling, and Fallback Policies Change Quadrotor Controller Comparisons: A Reproducible Simulation Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35165)**  `arXiv:2610.35165`  
  _Xuan-Quy Dao, Le-Minh Nguyen, Ngoc-Bich Le_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Quadrotor controller comparisons commonly report a single tracking error, although the ranking also depends on tuning effort, reference information, actuator prediction, optimizer fallback, and command timing. We quantify these effects for cascade PID, hover LQR, boundary-layer sliding-mode control (BL-SMC), linear MPC with LQR fallback (LMPC-F), a preview-enabled LMPC-F, and a geometric controller on a common nonlinear plant with rotor gyroscopic coupling, motor lag, and saturation. A primary study (556 episodes at 50~Hz) combines matched twelve-candidate tuning, 400 paired evaluation episodes, and a 48-cell MPC factorial; a confirmation study (1462 episodes) repeats the evaluation on 50 fresh realizations with tuning budgets of 12, 24, and 48 candidates. Matched tuning changed the mean-RMSE ordering of the fixed baseline settings, mainly by moving BL-SMC from last to first. The ordering recurred on fresh realizations and did not change with 48 candidates, although BL-SMC's lead there depends on a wider search range for one of its gains. Reference preview reduced MPC tracking error and removed fallback activity on the figure-eight task. In single abrupt-step runs, completion depended jointly on fallback policy, predictor, and actuator authority. Replaying measured command-call delays terminated three of four nominal MPC configurations on a desktop and all four on a Raspberry Pi~5, whereas capping the solver at 100 iterations removed every deadline miss in these profiles. We propose a reporting checklist that adds tuning effort, failure rates, fallback activity, applied-input variation, and command timing to tracking accuracy.
  </details>

- **[SimpleVLN: Towards Simple and Frontier Vision-Language Navigation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23203)**  `arXiv:2610.23203`  
  _Lingyi Hong, Weiren Cai, Jiayu Chen, Xinyu Zhou, Bailin He, Yunfei Guo, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) requires embodied agents to ground language in visual observations and make long-horizon decisions. Existing methods often address these demands through task-specific architectures. As multimodal large language models (MLLMs) become increasingly capable, an important question remains: Have we truly unlocked the potential of native MLLMs for VLN before introducing task-specific architecture? We present SimpleVLN, an architecture-preserving framework developed through studies of navigation formulation, data construction, and optimization. At the formulation level, SimpleVLN combines single-turn decision inputs with fixed-budget global-local memory to efficiently use navigation history without unbounded context growth, while action chunks enable efficient output of multiple primitive actions per model invocation. For data construction, we combine expert demonstrations with policy-dependent DAgger experience and develop a scalable synthesis pipeline that generates large-scale tasks for reinforcement learning. At the optimization level, a progressive IL-DAgger-RL pipeline advances from action imitation to task-level outcome optimization. Comprehensive experiments validate the effectiveness of these three aspects. We instantiate SimpleVLN across multiple MLLM backbones and model sizes, demonstrating its generality. SimpleVLN achieves 76.7% and 80.1% success rates on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE splits, respectively, substantially outperforming existing methods. These results show that the navigation capabilities of native MLLMs can be effectively unlocked without task-specific architectural designs.
  </details>

- **[Modular Inverse Dynamics and Wrench Recovery for Closed-Chain Mechanisms Using Path Assembly](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21400)**  `arXiv:2610.21400`  
  _Mohammad Dastranj, Jouni Mattila_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Rigid closed chains can admit indeterminate internal reactions even when their motion is fully specified. This paper develops a modular inverse-dynamics workflow that combines path-based motion reconstruction with recovery of uniquely determined actuator and joint-wrench outputs. Analytical second-order differentiation of assembled transformation paths supplies passive velocities and accelerations on a regular closure branch. Spatial Newton--Euler balances are then assembled over the physical body-and-joint graph. Established nullspace and dual criteria identify and recover unique outputs, while balance, ideal-joint admissibility and affine-family diagnostics assess nonunique reference reactions. Evaluation against Simscape Multibody uses prescribed motion of a seven-degree-of-freedom heavy-duty hybrid serial--parallel manipulator under common rigid-body, ideal-joint assumptions. The results show close agreement with the reference for passive positions, actuator efforts and uniquely recoverable constraint-wrench components. Reaction diagnostics support compatibility with the admissible numerical load family.
  </details>

- **[WorldOracle: Benchmarking Action-Conditioned World Models against Real-World Executions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18826)**  `arXiv:2610.18826`  
  _Haoyi Duan, Liliang Chen, Nan Wang, Yang Zhang, Yuhang Lu, Xiaotong Chen, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We introduce WorldOracle, a benchmark specifically designed to evaluate action-conditioned world models (ACWMs) against paired real-world executions. Given the same initial observation and low-level action sequence, WorldOracle asks whether a predicted rollout reproduces what happens in the real world, including physical consequences and task-state transitions. We evaluate models along four complementary dimensions: physical state correctness, interaction spatial alignment, key interaction area fidelity, and multi-view action coherence. To support this evaluation, we curate real-world training and evaluation suites that cover different interaction dynamics and embodiments. The evaluation suite contains long, multi-segment episodes with both successful and failed executions, enabling evaluation across varied action outcomes and behavior distributions. Experiments on seven representative ACWMs reveal distinct model strengths and failure modes. WorldOracle provides a systematic foundation for measuring and advancing action-conditioned world modeling for manipulation. We release the datasets, evaluation code, and leaderboard:this https URL.
  </details>

- **[Linear Recurrent Memory Suffices to Distil a World-Model Policy for Robot Air Hockey](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39151)**  `arXiv:2609.39151`  
  _F. Olivia Fan, Oliver Obst_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Does memory-dependent control need nonlinear recurrent dynamics? We study simulated air-hockey defence under temporary loss of puck tracking. A DreamerV3 teacher outperforms a memoryless policy under tracking loss, and erasing its recurrent state at the moment tracking fails cuts its save rate sharply, so the task requires memory. We distil this teacher into compact recurrent policies with a 64-dimensional state, combining a diagonal linear recurrence with an optional rank-$k$ nonlinear innovation while the observation encoder and action head stay nonlinear. Across five matched seeds, the purely linear recurrent model ($k=0$) matches both the GRU baseline and the teacher throughout the tested range of tracking loss. Increasing nonlinear innovation rank provides no measured benefit. This result comes from a fresh test split that was opened only after all models and analyses were frozen. Under 5\,mm observation noise, without retraining, the linear student keeps a higher save rate than the GRU baseline, while using fewer recurrent parameters and less computation. These results suggest that, for this memory-dependent control task, nonlinear representation learning around a simple linear memory can be sufficient, and that nonlinear recurrent dynamics are not necessarily required.
  </details>

- **[One from Infinity: Actualizing Futures from Pretrained World Models into Robot Actions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36413)**  `arXiv:2609.36413`  
  _Bang Du, Yichen Xie, Shuqi Zhao, Yuxin Chen, Menglin Wu, Masayoshi Tomizuka_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  A pretrained video world model admits many plausible futures for a scene, but a robot must realize the exact task-conditioned one. To turn world models into executable robot policies, existing methods fine-tune the heavy world model backbone using large-scale robot data and computational resources. Challenging this status quo, we argue that the expensive part has already been paid in the world model pretraining since the representation space of a video world model encoder lays out the diverse potential futures. In this case, what remains is to determine the future that accomplishes the task and to read out the actions that realize it. We formalize this task as actualization, which learns a task-conditioned realization on top of a prior supplied by a frozen world model encoder. This can be solved by a tiny actualizer model. We implement RoboActualizer with as few as 60M parameters on top of a frozen world model encoder. The actualizer is composed of two lightweight DiT experts that jointly predict future latents and actions by flow matching. The model can be trained entirely on a single GPU with 32 GB peak memory. With up to 100x fewer trainable parameters than existing WAMs and VLAs, RoboActualizer reaches great performance on simulation benchmarks including LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin 2.0 and five tasks on two real-world platforms, with a low latency of 39 ms that allows real-time control.
  </details>

- **[CommitFlow: Semantic Commitment Verification and Local Correction for Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation VLA Execution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.21908)**  `arXiv:2609.21908`  
  _Zixiang Zhao, Yansong Feng, Jibao Yuan, Yang Yang, Chaoyu Wang, Haoran Xiao, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Although vision-language-action (VLA) policies have advanced rapidly, long-horizon execution may still progress to the next task stage before the required physical effect has been established. We call this a mismatch between semantic commitments, physical conditions that a stage must establish or maintain, and the actual physical state. Because an action command alone cannot confirm such a condition, local deviations can propagate and cause task failure. To address this problem, we present CommitFlow, a closed-loop execution framework that combines commitment monitoring with local correction while keeping the base policy frozen. CommitFlow integrates three components. A Semantic Commitment Monitor (SCM) compares stage requirements against current state evidence and holds back dependent actions when a required condition is unmet or violated. BoundaryFlow then generates a local correction conditioned on the current state and base action, and Relation and Gain Calibration (RGC) selects the smallest correction strength that satisfies the relevant constraints. Across the ten common RoboTwin 2.0 benchmark tasks, CommitFlow achieves a mean success rate of 75.9 percent, improving on the base policy pi0.5 by 22.7 percent. Cross-policy experiments show consistent gains, pointing toward reliable long-horizon robot execution.
  </details>

- **[Navi-Agent: Unlocalized Monocular Navigation Agent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20388)**  `arXiv:2609.20388`  
  _Wenyuan Xie, Mengyang Hong, Yongzhong Wang, Yanbiao Ji, Yijin Zhou, Shaokai Wu, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Vision-Language Navigation in Continuous Environments (VLN-CE) requires an embodied agent to execute long-horizon instructions in unknown environments. Existing zero-shot VLN-CE systems typically maintain spatial states through geometric localization or coordinate-based representations. Recent geometry-constrained navigation removes depth and globally consistent coordinates, but maintaining persistent spatial awareness for place confirmation, progress verification, and recovery remains challenging. We present Navi-Agent, a zero-shot VLN-CE agent that constructs a coordinate-free spatial state from visual observations and executed motion histories. Navi-Agent organizes this state as a navigation topology, where nodes represent visual places and edges represent motion transitions. This representation enables observation-based approximate self-localization, task progress verification, and visual revisitation-based recovery. Navi-Agent performs closed-loop navigation by decomposing instructions into sub-goals, executing local visual navigation, and verifying visited places through the constructed spatial state. Experiments on zero-shot VLN-CE benchmark and real-world robot platforms show that Navi-Agent achieves state-of-the-art performance among geometry-constrained methods while remaining competitive with approaches relying on geometric localization.
  </details>

- **[HINT: Human-Intent Inception for Agentic Robot Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02653)**  `arXiv:2609.02653`  
  _Mingyu Mei, Haojie Xu, Shihao Jin, Zibo Dai, Qihao Cheng, Zhengrui Lv, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Humans can perform complex manipulations given a simple intent through an overall instruction, while continuously adapting to evolving visual observations. However, current vision-language action (VLA) models and other action policies struggle to realize this high-level intelligent behavior under dense, evolving visual inputs and sparse language guidance. Visual correlations can then dominate semantic intent, leading actions to follow visual shortcuts rather than human goals. We present HINT (Human-INTent INcepTion), an agentic framework inspired by the human manipulation principles: semantic intent changes sparsely at manipulation-pattern transitions, whereas continuous control primarily depends on the evolving object-hand relationship. HINT invokes semantic reasoning only at pattern transitions to resolve the current subtask and target, then maintains this commitment through multi-view grounding and visual tracking. We explore two visual interfaces-image-space semantic highlighting and attention-prior injection-to communicate the tracked intent to the action policy without introducing additional trainable parameters into the foundation action model. Experiments across three long-horizon tasks and out-of-distribution variants show that HINT substantially improves intent understanding, task progress, and end-to-end success across two foundation policies while preserving low-latency control. Project page:this https URL
  </details>

- **[Contact-Aided Factor-Graph Localization for Underwater Sampling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26932)**  `arXiv:2608.26932`  
  _Michele Grimaldi, Yosaku Maeda, Hitoshi Kakami, Ignacio Carlucho, Yvan R. Petillot, Tomoya Inoue_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Accurate state estimation for autonomous underwater vehicles performing close-range seafloor sampling remains challenging. In low-altitude operation, down-looking cameras over featureless planar seabeds produce scale ambiguity, lateral degeneracy, and inconsistent feature tracking. Meanwhile, inertial-Doppler Velocity Log (DVL) fusion alone provides no mechanism for structural drift correction. We propose a Contact-Aided Factor-Graph Localization framework that treats physical interaction as an informative geometric constraint within a smoothing-based localization formulation. The method tightly fuses suction-based manipulator contact events with adaptive visual odometry, learned object detections, and on-board sensors. Visual odometry relative-pose factors and landmark bearing-range factors are uncertainty-scaled according to inlier statistics to prevent visually weak frames from destabilizing the estimator, while contact events are modeled as high-confidence factors that induce implicit loop closures without appearance-based place recognition. Furthermore, the system can fully initialize online during motion. Experimental evaluation in tanks, harbor, and simulation environments demonstrates that contact-induced constraints significantly reduce trajectory drift and improve object revisit accuracy compared to filtering-based navigation and contact-free graph formulations. These results highlight the role of embodied physical interaction as a localization primitive in perception-degraded underwater environments
  </details>

- **[Communication in modular robotic motor control: Bilateral controllers under realistic constraints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13904)**  `arXiv:2608.13904`  
  _Jingwen Li, Levin Kuhlmann, Jason Friedman, Gideon Kowadlo_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Robotic motor control requires accurate movement and stable posture under signal-dependent noise and energetic constraints. Inspired by bilateral organisation in biological motor control, we study whether two recurrent controllers outperform a monolithic controller and how learned inter-module communication and its delay affect control. We train two GRU-based modules with a learnable, delayed communication channel in a two-arm musculoskeletal simulator. Success rate combines reaching accuracy (endpoint error below 2 cm) and holding stability (variance below 2.5e-5 m^2). The modular architecture achieves 87.6% +/- 13.8% success, compared with 68.9% +/- 27.8% for a parameter-matched monolithic controller. Within the communicating bilateral architecture, non-zero delays increase success rate by 11.3 percentage points and reduce energetic cost by approximately 17% relative to zero delay. Compared with a bilateral controller without communication, learned communication reduces endpoint and trajectory errors by approximately 27% and 52%, movement variance by 13%, and co-contraction index by 4%. These findings suggest that modular organisation supports motor control under noise and energetic constraints, while communication and its timing influence trade-offs among precision, stability, and energetic cost.
  </details>

- **[ContactGuard: Pre-Contact Execution Monitoring with Action-Conditioned Latent World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13438)**  `arXiv:2608.13438`  
  _Gehan Zheng, Matthew Johnson-Roberson, Weiming Zhi_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Contact-rich manipulation failures are often detected only after the robot has committed to contact. This is especially limiting in wrist-camera setups: close gripper--object views help observe contact, but a poor approach may already push, miss, slip, or disturb the object before conventional detectors react. We introduce ContactGuard, a pre-contact execution monitor for chunked visuomotor policies. Given the policy's planned action chunk, ContactGuard predicts its short-horizon consequence in latent visual space and aborts if the predicted future latent indicates likely failure. Its latent world model is trained from unlabelled robot trajectories to predict compact multi-view visual embeddings under planned actions, avoiding pixel-level video prediction. A lightweight failure probe is then trained from a small labelled set of pre-contact clips. At deployment, ContactGuard anchors prediction before an imminent contact event, rolls the model forward under the policy's own actions, and verifies the predicted post-contact latent. Across real-world contact-rich manipulation tasks, ContactGuard consistently benefits from action-conditioned latent prediction over current-state and direct-prediction alternatives. Counterfactual action perturbations further show that its failure score responds to the specific action being proposed. We deploy the same frozen monitor online with the visuomotor policy, where it provides a pre-contact abort signal without modifying the underlying policy.
  </details>

- **[Predictive safety filter enhanced curriculum learning control for efficient vehicle dynamics controller](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09653)**  `arXiv:2608.09653`  
  _Baocong Zhang, Siliang Lu, Chenyang Li_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Recent advances in learning-based control have enabled impressive achievements in solving complex control problems in various domains. However, since learning-based control may not be able to realize safety-guaranties, it is of great importance to enhance safety and robustness while maintaining good performances. Take vehicle motion \& dynamics control as an example, in order to overcome the pain points of traditional methods such as heavy parameter calibration effort and learning-based control to bring better performance and efficiency in stability \& agility over prior work for state-based vehicle control tasks, in this work, our method aims to develop a curriculum learning controller enhanced with physics-based predictive safety filter. The validation is conducted with the Python-CarSim platform, demonstrating better improvements and scalability under various maneuvers.
  </details>

- **[From Uncertainty to Determinism: Coarse-to-Fine Visual Floorplan Localization without Ray Matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26817)**  `arXiv:2607.26817`  
  _Shiyong Meng, Bolei Chen, Ping Zhong, Yang Wan, Rongzhi Wang, Jiazhi Xia, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Visual Floorplan Localization (FLoc) has emerged as a promising solution for indoor localization by matching egocentric images against minimalist structural maps. However, due to cross-modal information asymmetry and repetitive indoor layouts, visual FLoc is fundamentally challenged by multimodal pose distributions, where visually identical observations map to distinct, spatially separated locations. Existing ray-matching-based methods tackle this by explicitly predicting sparse geometric or semantic rays, which inherently incur information loss and demand resource-intensive preprocessing alongside exhaustive matching during inference. In this paper, we bypass the intermediate ray-matching paradigm and propose a coarse-to-fine visual FLoc framework that progresses from uncertainty to determinism. In the coarse stage, we design an image-conditioned pose diffusion model to parameterize the continuous multimodal pose distribution, effectively routing stochastically initialized pose particles toward distinct candidate modes. In the refinement stage, we propose a localized refiner that predicts bounded sub-meter pose residuals from candidate-centered floorplan crops, where structural ambiguities are largely eliminated. Our method effectively balances global multi-hypothesis tracking and local sub-meter refinement without requiring any offline map preprocessing or test-time lookup tables. Comprehensive results on the S3D (full) and ZInD benchmarks demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art accuracy and robustness.
  </details>

- **[GRACE: Gradient-Free Robot Action Generation via Combined Diffusion-MPPI Posterior Mean Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21661)**  `arXiv:2607.21661`  
  _Leesai Park, Jiho Hong, Sanghyun Kim_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Diffusion policies generate multimodal robot action sequences from demonstrations, but steering them toward deployment-time constraints typically relies on differentiable guidance costs. This excludes many practical safety constraints, such as binary collision checks, joint limits, and black-box rollout costs that are nondifferentiable. We propose Gradient-free Robot Action generation via Combined diffusion-MPPI posterior mean Estimation (GRACE), which guides a pretrained diffusion policy with Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control using only forward cost evaluations. Building on the common score-ascent structure of diffusion and MPPI, GRACE constructs a cost-conditioned guidance posterior at each reverse step and estimates its mean with a single MPPI update centered at the diffusion reverse mean. For differentiable costs, GRACE recovers conventional gradient guidance under a first-order, matched-covariance approximation. GRACE attains higher success rates than diffusion-based and sampling-based baselines in simulation. On a real 7-DoF manipulator, GRACE achieves 43/45 successes without obstacle collisions, compared with 17/45 for the unguided prior. Code and experiment videos are available atthis https URL.

- **[MorphQuad: Morphable Quadrotor for Superhuman Maneuverability, Manipulation, and Resiliency](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02764)**  `arXiv:2607.02764`  
  _Jose Diaz Peon Gonzalez Pacheco, Jiawei Xu, Andrew Zhao, Hongyu Zhou, Atharva Navsalkar, Andrew Scheffer, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Infrastructure maintenance, contact-based inspection, and emergency response can benefit from aerial vehicles that act as a flying human hand with extreme maneuverability, manipulation, and resiliency (MMR): maneuverability to fly in arbitrary orientations; manipulation to point sensors, turn valves, and press tools at arbitrary orientations; resiliency to maintain motion accuracy and force application despite disturbances from arbitrary directions, such as wind, ground effects, and friction. Realizing MMR requires more than omnidirectional flight; it also requires (I) vectoring of maximum thrust in any direction, (II) almost-everywhere stability, accounting for kinematic singularities, control singularities, and inter-rotor downwash interference, and (III) miniaturizable structural designs. Existing aerial vehicles satisfy a subset of I--III. On hardware, MorphQuad preserves a planar quadrotor structure, and independently articulates each of the four rotor systems, eliminating control singularities and enabling all rotors to align and vector the platform's maximum thrust in any direction; on control and thrust allocation, MorphQuad enjoys a closed-form null-space correction for gimbal lock and downwash interference that maintains almost-everywhere stability via coupling with a generalized geometric controller. With fully-onboard computation, localization, and trajectory execution, MorphQuad demonstrates continuous multi-revolution rotation while translating or hovering (maneuverability); valve turning, perching, and object pressing and pushing with human-wrist strength (manipulation); and push-pull recovery and wind rejection, even when directed to a single rotor (resiliency).

- **[Stable Transformer-Actor-Critic Model Predictive Control: A Contraction Analysis Approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20197)**  `arXiv:2606.20197`  
  _Antonio Marino, Valerio Modugno, Marco Cognetti_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Hybrid optimization-learning frameworks, such as Actor-Critic Model Predictive Control (MPC), rely on dynamically adjusting cost parameters to manage complex control landscapes. In this paper, we introduce a certifiably robust Transformer-Actor-Critic MPC architecture that leverages history-aware sequence models to shape local optimization while maintaining strict physical safety guarantees. First, we mathematically constrain the Transformer sequence models to satisfy global incremental Input-to-State Stability ($\delta$ISS). Second, we integrate these neural Lipschitz bounds with Riemannian contraction theory, deriving a novel coupled small-gain condition that enforces uniform closed-loop contraction stability across the interconnected system. Evaluated on quadrotor control and decentralized multi-agent navigation tasks subjected to severe observation noise and process disturbances, our closed-loop stable formulation successfully translates theoretical bounds into physical safety.
  </details>

- **[VANDERER: Map-Free Exploration using Future-Aware and Visual-Curiosity-Guided Diffusion Policy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.14879)**  `arXiv:2606.14879`  
  _Venkata Naren Devarakonda, Raktim Gautam Goswami, Prashanth Krishnamurthy, Farshad Khorrami_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Mobile agents require efficient exploration strategies to map unseen environments and autonomously plan tasks. Traditional methods rely on generating occupancy maps and optimizing the sequence in which unexplored regions are visited. However, beyond requiring additional sensor suites for reliable pose and depth estimation, occupancy map-based exploration policies often neglect environmental traversability constraints. To address these limitations, we propose VANDERER, an exploration framework that leverages a Visual Curiosity Module (VCM) to guide pre-trained diffusion policies using only monocular image data. This curiosity module predicts the outcomes of proposed actions via a navigation world model and evaluates them through a curiosity cost. The cost then guides the diffusion process toward generating actions that maximize exploration. Evaluated across diverse simulated environments, VANDERER outperforms established baselines, achieving $2.3\times$ the exploration efficiency of Frontier Search. Our results reveal a correlation between visual and geometric curiosity in outdoor environments, demonstrating that VANDERER can effectively leverage this relationship for efficient exploration using simple robotic setups.
  </details>

- **[Flying on Imagination: DreamerV3-Style World Models under Environment Distribution Shift for Quadrotor Navigation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05015)**  `arXiv:2606.05015`  
  _Luca Zanatta, Grzegorz Malczyk, Kostas Alexis_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  DreamerV3-style reconstructive world models offer a route to vision-based navigation for aerial robots through learned latent dynamics. Yet their behavior under shifts in the training environment and their ability to support navigation using imagined observations, predictions generated by rolling the latent dynamics forward without new sensory input, remain insufficiently characterized. We study four training-environment regimes for depth-based quadrotor navigation, spanning a fixed layout, a finite set of layouts, low-discrepancy continuous obstacle sampling, and i.i.d. uniform sampling. We cross-evaluate reconstruction before and after Reinforcement Learning fine-tuning, separately evaluate the resulting policies in simulation, and transfer them to a real quadrotor without real-world fine-tuning. We demonstrate onboard flight driven by imagined state and depth: a 24.7m mission in which 66% of flight time and 76% of traveled distance occur during repeated 5s sensor-free imagination windows, with prediction quality degrading over each open-loop interval and recovering after sensory re-grounding. Additionally, in closed-loop hardware transfer, all policies succeed in a setting close to the simulated geometry, whereas the policy trained from a single fixed layout fails under a corridor-topology and obstacle-type shift, while the other three succeed.
  </details>

- **[Simulation-Informed Diffusion for Decentralized Multi-robot Motion Planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.27697)**  `arXiv:2605.27697`  
  _Jinhao Liang, Sven Koenig, Ferdinando Fioretto_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Decentralized multi-robot motion planning requires each robot to generate collision-free trajectories from local observations, without global sensing or reliable communication. However, most existing planners, whether classical or learning-based, generate trajectories from a static snapshot of the local observation, which limits their ability to anticipate the future behavior of neighboring robots. This limitation is critical as the number of robots increases and the environment becomes more cluttered. Motivated by world models that use future state estimation to improve planning decisions, this paper introduces Simulation-Informed Diffusion (SID), a decentralized framework built on constraint-aware diffusion models (CADM) that simulate neighboring robots' future trajectories to guide each robot's own planning. SID first uses CADM to simulate the future trajectories of neighboring robots from their currently observed states, and then uses the same CADM to plan each robot's own trajectory under safety constraints informed by these simulations. Crucially, the accurate simulation of neighbors enables a minimal communication scheme that triggers coordination only when necessary in highly congested scenarios. Experiments across diverse environments show that SID consistently outperforms baseline methods in terms of planning effectiveness and constraint satisfaction, and scales to scenarios with 108 robots and 160 obstacles.
  </details>

- **[Collaborative Navigation and Exploration with $β$-Sparse Gaussian Processes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.26304)**  `arXiv:2605.26304`  
  _Evangelos Psomiadis, Dipankar Maity, Panagiotis Tsiotras_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Collaborative navigation of heterogeneous robots in unknown environments poses significant challenges due to sensing, communication, and computational limitations. In this work, a lead robot navigates toward a target with the assistance of a mobile sensor robot (e.g., an airborne drone), whose task is to explore the environment and communicate relevant map information under bandwidth constraints. We propose a framework in which the sensor determines both which map regions to transmit and which navigation action to execute online, while also predicting unexplored regions of the environment. To this end, we present $\beta$-Sparse Gaussian Processes, a variational sparse Gaussian Process (GP) model for task-aware inducing point selection under cardinality constraints. Furthermore, we develop an action-selection strategy that balances task relevance with exploration. Simulations on Mars and Earth maps show that the proposed framework outperforms all considered bandwidth-constrained baselines, reducing accumulated path cost by approximately 35% compared to no communication, while decreasing transmitted information by 94% relative to the full-information GP baseline. The results further highlight the benefits of GP-based map prediction over methods without prediction, as well as the advantages of navigation-aware region selection over approaches that do not prioritize task-relevant regions.
  </details>

- **[DSSP: Diffusion State Space Policy with Full-History Encoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.14598)**  `arXiv:2605.14598`  
  _Zhiyuan Guan, Jianshu Hu, Han Fang, Yunpeng Jiang, Yize Huang, Shujia Li, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Diffusion-based imitation learning has shown strong promise for robot manipulation. However, most existing policies condition only on the current observation or a short window of recent observations, limiting their ability to resolve history-dependent ambiguities in long-horizon tasks. To address this, we introduce \ours, a history-conditioned Diffusion State Space Policy that enables efficient, full-history conditioning for robot manipulation. Leveraging the continuous sequence modeling properties of State Space Models (SSMs), our history encoder effectively compresses the entire observation stream into a compact context representation. To ensure this context preserves critical information regarding future state evolution, the encoder is optimized with a dynamics-aware auxiliary training objective. This high-level context representation is then seamlessly fused with recent state observations to form a hierarchical conditioning mechanism for action generation. Furthermore, to maintain architectural consistency and minimize GPU memory overhead, we also instantiate the diffusion backbone itself using an SSM. Extensive experiments across simulation benchmarks and real-world manipulation tasks show that \ours achieves state-of-the-art performance with a significantly smaller model size, demonstrating superior efficiency of the hierarchical conditioning in capturing crucial information as the history length increases. Project page:this https URL
  </details>

- **[OA-WAM: Object-Addressable World Action Model for Robust Robot Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06481)**  `arXiv:2605.06481`  
  _Yushan Liu, Peibo Sun, Shoujie Li, Yifan Xie, Lingfeng Zhang, Xintao Chao, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  World action models (WAMs) learn manipulation by predicting actions and future observations, yet their success drops sharply when the camera viewpoint, object layout or robot initial state changes. Such changes keep the instructed object the same but alter the appearance and pose features the policy observes, which in standard attention also form the keys that locate the object. We introduce OA-WAM, an object-addressable WAM that finds each object by an identity address fixed for the episode and reads its changing state. In every layer of a pretrained multimodal trunk, object-slot keys depend only on the address and frame position, and values carry the current state; the same addresses key the action pointer and index per-object forecasts, which can trigger re-grounding. Fine-tuned on standard LIBERO demonstrations, OA-WAM transfers zero-shot to LIBERO-Plus with 90.5% success, outperforming all ten published baselines. It also leads on LIBERO (99.0%) and, fine-tuned on BridgeData V2, on SimplerEnv WidowX (88.9%). On five real-robot tasks, it succeeds in 89 of 100 nominal trials, versus 73 for the strongest baseline. Ablations trace its robustness to addressing rather than to object slots: with standard attention, slots do no better than a slot-free policy, and addressing them by identity raises geometric success by 10.7 points. Forecasting the addressed objects is likewise a stronger training signal than forecasting image codes.
  </details>

- **[LLM-Flax: LLM-Generated Rules and Object Guidance for Neuro-Symbolic Task Planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.26569)**  `arXiv:2604.26569`  
  _Seongmin Kim, Daegyu Lee_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Adapting a neuro-symbolic task planner to a new domain can require hand-authored symbolic rules and solved training instances for a learned object scorer. This paper presents LLM-Flax, which applies large language models (LLMs) to offline rule generation, failure recovery, and object scoring within the Flax planning pipeline. Generated rules undergo validation and corrective feedback before reuse, while runtime guidance operates within a shared planning budget. Experiments on MazeNamo and two additional domains show that the evaluated rule configuration improves planning success over manually authored rules while retaining the trained object scorer. Across eight MazeNamo settings, the mean success rate increases by approximately three percentage points. Controlled comparisons distinguish the effects of rule content from the choice of generator. Runtime recovery and object scoring do not establish an overall performance advantage under the evaluated planning budgets. These findings demonstrate the value of reusable LLM-generated rules and identify information quality and inference efficiency as central challenges for runtime guidance.
  </details>

- **[Asymptotically Stable Gait Generation and Instantaneous Walkability Determination for Planar Almost Linear Biped with Knees](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.12274)**  `arXiv:2604.12274`  
  _Fumihiko Asano, Ning Lei, Taiki Sedoguchi_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  A class of planar bipedal robots with unique mechanical properties has been proposed, where all links are balanced around the hip joint, preventing natural swinging motion due to gravity. A common property of their equations of motion is that the inertia matrix is a constant matrix, there are no nonlinear velocity terms, and the gravity term contains simple nonlinear terms. By performing a Taylor expansion of the gravity term and making a linear approximation, it is easy to derive a linearized model, and calculations for future states or walkability determination can be performed instantaneously without the need for numerical integration. This paper extends the method to a planar biped robot model with knees. First, we derive the equations of motion, constraint conditions, and inelastic collisions for a planar 6-DOF biped robot, design its control system, and numerically generate a stable bipedal gait on a horizontal plane. Next, we reduce the equations of motion to a 3-DOF model, and derive a linearized model by approximating the gravity term as linear around the expansion point for the thigh frame angle. Through numerical simulations, we demonstrate that calculations for future states and walkability determination can be completed in negligible time. By applying control inputs to the obtained model, performing state-space realization, and then discretizing it, instantaneous walkability determination through iterative calculation becomes possible. Through detailed gait analysis, we discuss how the knee joint flexion angle and the expansion point affect the accuracy of the linear approximation, and the issues that arise when descending a small step.
  </details>

- **[Designing and Validating a Self-Aligning Tool Changer for Modular Reconfigurable Manipulation Robots](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.04760)**  `arXiv:2603.04760`  
  _Mahfudz Maskur, Takuya Kiyokawa, Kensuke Harada_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Modular reconfigurable robots require reliable mechanisms for automated tool exchange, but conventional rigid active couplings often fail due to inevitable positioning and orientational errors. To address this, we propose a misalignment-tolerant tool changer. The tool changer consists of an insert part on the robot side, which contains a servo-driven cam and lock-pin, and a receptacle part on the tool side, which has an isosceles triangular lead-in guide and chamfered walls. During insertion, these geometries generate angled contact forces that passively align the two parts, so the tool changer compensates for angular and lateral misalignments without force sensors. A motor-driven rotating tool exchange station stores the tools and rotates to bring the selected tool to the exchange position. Experiments confirmed that, with the current guide and chamfer geometry, the tool changer tolerates rotational offsets of $ \pm$ 20 degrees and lateral offsets of up to 7 mm.
  </details>

- **[Gait Generation Balancing Joint Load and Mobility for Legged Modular Robots with Easily Detachable Joints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.04757)**  `arXiv:2603.04757`  
  _Kennosuke Chihara, Takuya Kiyokawa, Tetsuya Shitara, Kensuke Harada_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Modular robots can adapt their morphology to diverse tasks, but locomotion can impose large loads on detachable joints. This paper presents an NSGA-III-based multi-objective gait optimization framework with three objectives: a locomotion speed, a static stability, and a normalized joint-load metric based on joint reaction forces. The framework yields nondominated gait candidates that reveal the trade-offs among these objectives. In a flat-terrain comparison using the 6-legged tetrapod gait, adding the joint-load objective reduced the mean maximum joint reaction force by 11.5% and increased the mean minimum stability by 41.2%, while decreasing the mean forward speed by 10.5%. Simulations under flat, slope, and step conditions showed that locomotion feasibility depended on the combination of robot configuration, gait, and terrain. In physical experiments, the 4-legged trot completed locomotion on flat terrain and a 10 degrees slope, whereas the 6-legged tetrapod and tripod completed locomotion on flat terrain. These results demonstrate the feasibility of joint-load-aware gait generation based on explicit trade-offs among the three evaluated quantities
  </details>

- **[NestRL: A Nested Training Regime for Mutual Adaptation in Human-AI Teaming](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.17737)**  `arXiv:2602.17737`  
  _Upasana Biswas, Durgesh Kalwar, Subbarao Kambhampati, Sarath Sreedharan_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Mutual adaptation is a central challenge in human-AI teaming, as humans naturally adjust their strategies in response to an AI agent's behavior. Existing approaches attempt to approximate human behavior by diversifying training partners; however, these partners are typically static and fail to capture the adaptive nature of human teammates. When agents are trained jointly in standard multi-agent settings, they often converge to opaque coordination strategies that work only with their co-trained partners, leading to poor generalization. To model adaptive human behavior, we formulate human-AI teaming as an Interactive Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (I-POMDP). We propose NestRL, a nested training regime that learns the solution to a finite-level I-POMDP by training agents at each level against adaptive agents from the level below. This exposes agents to adaptive behavior while preventing emergence of opaque coordination strategies. We provide theoretical analysis showing that NestRL agents avoid convergence to partner-specific strategies, and validate this empirically in the Overcooked domain against state-of-the-art baselines. NestRL achieves higher task performance with both unseen adaptive agents and real human teammates, while exhibiting significantly greater adaptability over the course of interaction.
  </details>

- **[Illumination-Robust Localization around Unknown Space Objects using Multispectral Image Fusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.12203)**  `arXiv:2512.12203`  
  _Eric J. Elias, Michael Esswein, Jonathan P. How, David W. Miller_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  As on-orbit operations grow, so does the need for precise navigation around unknown resident space objects (RSOs), such as spacecraft, debris, and asteroids. Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) algorithms are often studied for mapping an RSO and estimating the inspector's relative pose, but conventional cameras struggle during eclipse, while lidar, though illumination-robust, has higher SWaP. Thermal-infrared cameras track targets through difficult lighting but lack the resolution and feature-richness of visible cameras. Images of a target satellite in low Earth orbit are simulated in both visible and thermal bands, and fused at the pixel level to combine each sensor's strengths for front-end tracking. Thermal imagery is further exploited by a novel silhouette-based visual place recognition (VPR) method that detects loop closures without training, runs entirely on CPU, and outperforms all baselines. Integrated SLAM performance is compared using visible, thermal-infrared, and fused imagery across lighting conditions, trajectories, and place recognition methods; using fused imagery for front-end tracking and our thermal-silhouette place recognition method performs best. The results show that visible and thermal modalities each provide unique information that is exploited differently at various stages of navigation. These low-SWaP sensors could ultimately enable reliable proximity operations on smaller, lower-cost spacecraft.
  </details>

- **[Controllable Generative Trajectory Prediction via Weak Preference Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.10731)**  `arXiv:2510.10731`  
  _Yongxi Cao, Julian F. Schumann, Jens Kober, Joni Pajarinen, Arkady Zgonnikov_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Deep generative models such as conditional variational autoencoders (CVAEs) have shown great promise for predicting trajectories of surrounding agents in autonomous vehicle planning. State-of-the-art models have achieved remarkable accuracy in such prediction tasks. Besides accuracy, diversity is also crucial for safe planning because human behaviors are inherently uncertain and multimodal. However, existing methods generally lack a scheme to generate controllably diverse trajectories, which is arguably more useful than randomly diversified trajectories, to the end of safe planning. To address this, we propose PrefCVAE, an augmented CVAE framework that uses weakly labeled preference pairs to imbue latent variables with semantic attributes. Using average velocity as an example attribute, we demonstrate that PrefCVAE enables controllable, semantically meaningful predictions without degrading baseline accuracy. Our results show the effectiveness of preference supervision as a cost-effective way to enhance sampling-based generative models.
  </details>

- **[Learning Latent Volumetric Dynamics for Multimodal Goal-Conditioned Robot Manipulation of Hair](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.06199)**  `arXiv:2510.06199`  
  _Chengyang Zhao, Uksang Yoo, Arkadeep Narayan Chaudhury, Giljoo Nam, Nathan Dennler, Andreea Bobu, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Hair care is an essential daily activity for many, yet it remains inaccessible to individuals with limited mobility and challenging for robot systems due to the fine-grained physical structure and complex dynamics of hair. In this work, we present DYMO-Hair, a model-based robot hair care system for generalizable multimodal goal-conditioned hair styling. We introduce a volumetric dynamics learning method that models combing-induced hair deformations through action-conditioned editing in a pre-trained hierarchical 3D latent space. This latent space captures diverse hair states through volumetric occupancy and local strand orientations, while large-scale pre-training, supported by a physics-based hair-combing simulator, enables generalization to previously unseen hairstyles. Coupled with a Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) planner, the learned dynamics model enables closed-loop hair styling toward both visual references and natural language instructions as user input. In closed-loop experiments, DYMO-Hair achieves lower geometric error than baseline systems for visual goals and receives significantly higher ratings than VLM-based planners for language goals in a 58-participant user study. Real-world experiments further demonstrate zero-shot transfer to seven physical wigs varying in color, length, and texture, effectively styling hair toward both visual and language goals without real-world fine-tuning. Together, these results represent a step toward more generalizable, flexible, and accessible robot hair styling in the real world. More details are available on:this https URL.
  </details>

- **[Two stage GNSS outlier detection for factor graph optimization based GNSS-RTK/INS/odometer fusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.00524)**  `arXiv:2510.00524`  
  _Baoshan Song, Penggao Yan, Xiao Xia, Yihan Zhong, Yuan Li, Weisong Wen, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  GNSS pseudorange outliers severely disturb carrier-phase ambiguity resolution and positioning, particularly during signal blockages and recovery. Temporal Doppler consistency provides a reliable short-term range-change reference, but requires valid measurements at both endpoints and becomes unavailable upon signal re-acquisition. This paper presents a two-stage pseudorange screening framework that complements Doppler consistency with joint IMU-odometer motion prediction. The second stage compares predicted and measured temporal changes of double-differenced pseudoranges against an accepted anchor epoch without using current GNSS observations in the motion reference. A first-order error model separates anchor, relative-motion, and measurement uncertainties to propagate factor-graph covariance into the chi-square detection gate, and both stages adjust code weights through a closed-form minimum-inflation rule. Under continuous tracking, Doppler screening reduces RTK 3D RMSE by 96.18% and outperforms the a-contrario baseline by 58.56%. When Doppler checks are unavailable, joint IMU-odometer prediction detects a 10-m outlier change in 99.58% of trials after 30 s and 73.72% after 60 s, reducing RIO 3D RMSE by up to 78.51% after outages while RI screening outperforms an inertial-aided baseline by 70.42% in simulation and 39.11% in deep urban canyons.
  </details>

- **[WiFi-based Global Localization in Large-Scale Environments Leveraging Structural Priors from osmAG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.10144)**  `arXiv:2508.10144`  
  _Xu Ma, Jiajie Zhang, Fujing Xie, Sören Schwertfeger_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  WiFi localization offers a lightweight global prior for robots in GPS-denied environments, but fingerprinting requires dense surveys and generalizes poorly beyond surveyed areas. We model received signal strength indicator (RSSI) measurements using OpenStreetMap Area Graph (osmAG) structural priors. Offline, known anchor access points (APs) support sequential calibration of line-of-sight (LOS) propagation and wall attenuation; unknown AP locations are then estimated by alternating ray-wall intersection checks, signal compensation, and least-squares fitting. The resulting AP map supports online robot position estimation using the same structure-aware model. In experiments in an 11,025~m$^2$ multi-floor environment, our method reduces the mean AP localization error from 5.86~m to 3.79~m. Mean robot localization errors are 3.12~m in fingerprinted areas and 3.83~m in unfingerprinted areas, where four baselines yield 11.00--20.21~m. The WiFi-related map representation achieves approximately 251:1 compression relative to the raw fingerprint database. These results support structural modeling for compact global localization beyond surveyed regions. Code and data:this https URL
  </details>

- **[Learned Controllers for Agile Quadrotors in Pursuit-Evasion Games](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.02849)**  `arXiv:2506.02849`  
  _Alejandro Sanchez Roncero, Yixi Cai, Olov Andersson, Petter Ogren_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We study one-versus-one (1v1) quadrotor pursuit-evasion, where a pursuer and an evader are trained with reinforcement learning (RL). Direct adversarial RL tends to be unstable because opponent policies change during training, causing non-stationarity, forgetting, and strategy cycling. We propose Asynchronous Multi-Stage Population-Based training, inspired by Policy-Space Response Oracles (PSRO). Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) trains responses against previously learned opponents held fixed during each stage. The uniform variant, AMSPB-U, samples opponents equally, while AMSPB-P combines hard prioritized fictitious self-play (PFSP) with uniform exploration to emphasize currently difficult opponents. In cross-evaluations against learned opponents, both variants improve pursuit-evasion balance over latest-opponent training. AMSPB-P scores highest while retaining competence against earlier strategies. Across varied starting positions and after larger-arena retraining, both population variants retain higher average success across the two roles than latest-opponent training. Hardware experiments with two 10 cm, approximately 40 g Crazyflie brushless quadrotors demonstrate zero-shot sim-to-real transfer against baseline controllers and learned adversaries across 42 flights. Recorded flights include captures of evaders reaching robust peak speeds of 3.31 m/s and accelerations of 17.95 m/s^2, with pursuer flight speeds up to 4.87 m/s.
  </details>

- **[Learning-based Autonomous Oversteer Control and Collision Avoidance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.15275)**  `arXiv:2505.15275`  
  _Seokjun Lee, Seung-Hyun Kong_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Oversteer, wherein a vehicle's rear tires lose traction and induce unintentional excessive yaw, poses critical safety challenges. Failing to control oversteer often leads to severe traffic accidents. Although recent autonomous driving efforts have attempted to handle oversteer through stabilizing maneuvers, the majority rely on expert-defined trajectories or assume obstacle-free environments, limiting real-world applicability. This paper introduces a novel end-to-end (E2E) autonomous driving approach that tackles oversteer control and collision avoidance simultaneously. Existing E2E techniques, including Imitation Learning (IL), Reinforcement Learning (RL), and Hybrid Learning (HL), generally require near-optimal demonstrations or extensive experience. Yet even skilled human drivers struggle to provide perfect demonstrations under oversteer, and high transition variance hinders the accumulation of sufficient data. Hence, we present Q-Compared Soft Actor-Critic (QC-SAC), a new HL algorithm that effectively learns from immature demonstration data and adapts rapidly to new conditions. To evaluate QC-SAC, we introduce a benchmark inspired by real-world driver training: a vehicle encounters sudden oversteer on a slippery surface and must avoid randomly placed obstacles ahead. Experimental results show that QC-SAC attains near-optimal driving policies, significantly surpassing state-of-the-art IL, RL, and HL baselines. Hardware-in-the-loop simulation (HILS) validation with physical steering hardware further demonstrates that QC-SAC can operate beyond a software-only simulation, providing an intermediate validation step toward real-vehicle implementation. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work that achieves safe autonomous control of vehicles in oversteer while simultaneously avoiding obstacles.
  </details>

- **[Training-free Task-oriented Grasp Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.04873)**  `arXiv:2502.04873`  
  _Jiaming Wang, Jizhuo Chen, Diwen Liu, Harold Soh_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  This paper presents a training-free pipeline for task-oriented grasp generation that combines pre-trained grasp generation models with vision-language models (VLMs). Unlike traditional approaches that focus solely on stable grasps, our method incorporates task-specific requirements by leveraging the semantic reasoning capabilities of VLMs. We evaluate five querying strategies, each utilizing different visual representations of candidate grasps, and demonstrate significant improvements over a baseline method in both grasp success and task compliance rates, with absolute gains of up to 36.9\% in overall success rate. Our results underline the potential of VLMs to enhance task-oriented manipulation, providing insights for future research in robotic grasping and human-robot interaction.
  </details>

- **[TARGO and TARGO-Net: Benchmarking Target-driven Object Grasping under Occlusions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.06168)**  `arXiv:2407.06168`  
  _Yan Xia, Ran Ding, Ziyuan Qin, Guanqi Zhan, Kaichen Zhou, Long Yang, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Predicting 6-DoF grasp poses from a single RGB-D frame has recently achieved impressive accuracy, yet performance can degrade significantly when the target object is heavily occluded by clutter. In this paper, we establish TARGO, the first benchmark dataset for TARget-driven Grasping under Occlusions, and introduce TARGO-Net, a grasp prediction model designed for visual occlusion. Our main contributions are fourfold: 1) We identify the visual occlusion challenge in single-view RGB-D 6-DoF grasping and show that current state-of-the-art models still suffer under severe occlusion. 2) We propose the TARGO dataset, which supports training and testing 6-DoF grasp models across different visual occlusion levels and enables robustness evaluation in real-world scenarios. 3) We devise TARGO-Net, a transformer-based grasping model with a target completion module and target-scene cross-attention, which achieves the most robust performance across all visual occlusion levels. 4) We show that target completion, number of occluders, and target minimum dimension also relate to grasp success in addition to visual occlusion.
  </details>
